title: Spin the carousel
statement: A carousel holds n horses, each tagged with a number. One spin moves every horse one seat to the right, and the horse in the last seat wraps to seat 0. Given the tags and a number of spins k, print the tags after k spins.
input: Line 1: n integers; line 2: the integer k.
output: n integers separated by spaces.

examples.why: The last two tags wrap around to the front.
k=4 on 3 seats is the same as k=1, so only the last tag wraps.

hints: Spinning n times returns to the start, so reduce k modulo n.
The answer is the last k items followed by the first n-k items.
approach: Reduce k modulo n, then output the slice of the last k elements followed by the first n-k elements. This avoids simulating individual spins.
edgeCases: k is a multiple of n

title: Sweep the zeros to the back
statement: A cashier has a row of coin counts, and some slots are empty (0). Slide all the non-empty counts to the front while keeping their relative order, and push every 0 to the end of the row.
input: One line of n integers.
output: The rearranged row as n integers.

examples.why: 3, 4, 5 keep their order; the two zeros go last.
The single 1 moves to the front.

hints: Keep a write position for the next non-zero value.
After copying all non-zeros forward, fill the rest with zeros.
approach: Scan once with a write index, copying each non-zero value to the write index and advancing it. Fill the remaining positions with zeros.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (in place)

title: Find the runner-up score
statement: A game logs the scores of n rounds. The runner-up is the second largest distinct score. Print it, or -1 if every round has the same score.
input: One line of n integers.
output: One integer.

examples.why: 9 is the best (twice); the next distinct value is 4.
Only one distinct value exists, so there is no runner-up.

hints: Duplicates of the maximum do not count as the runner-up.
Track the best and the second best in one pass, updating only on strictly greater/lesser values.
approach: Keep two variables, best and second, initialised to negative infinity. For each value, if it exceeds best shift best into second; else if it is between second and best (strictly) update second.

title: Skyline leaders
statement: Buildings stand in a row from west to east. A building is a leader if it is strictly taller than every building to its east (the easternmost building is always a leader). Print the heights of all leaders from west to east.
input: One line of n building heights.
output: Leader heights from west to east, space separated.

examples.why: 17 beats everything to its right; 5 beats 2; 2 is last.
The middle 4 is not strictly taller than the final 4, so it is not a leader.

hints: Think about scanning from the east end instead.
Keep the maximum seen so far while walking west; a new strict maximum is a leader.
approach: Walk from right to left maintaining the running maximum. Whenever the current height is strictly greater than that maximum, record it and update the maximum, then reverse the recorded list.

title: Tidy the sorted ledger
statement: A ledger lists invoice numbers in non-decreasing order, so repeats sit next to each other. Print the ledger with each number appearing only once, still in order.
input: One line of n sorted integers.
output: The deduplicated list, space separated.

examples.why: Each run of equal numbers collapses to one.

hints: Equal numbers are adjacent, so compare with the previous kept number.
Use a write pointer to do it in place.
approach: Because equal values are adjacent, keep an element only if it differs from the last kept one. A write index allows doing it in place.

title: The missing badge
statement: Badges are numbered 0 through n, but only n of them were handed out, each at most once. Given the numbers handed out in arbitrary order, print the one badge number that was not given.
input: One line of n distinct integers, each in 0..n.
output: The missing integer.

examples.why: n=3 so badges 0..3 exist; 2 is absent.
n=4 so badges 0..4 exist; 4 is absent.

hints: Compare against the sum of 0..n.
n(n+1)/2 minus the actual sum gives the answer (or XOR everything).
approach: The sum of 0..n is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the sum of the given numbers to get the missing badge.

title: Landslide winner
statement: In a vote, each ballot names a candidate by id. It is guaranteed that one candidate received strictly more than half of all ballots. Find that candidate using constant extra memory.
input: One line of n candidate ids.
output: The winning id.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5; ids fit in 32-bit; a majority winner exists
hints: A true majority cannot be cancelled out by pairing it off with different ids.
Keep a candidate and a counter: same id +1, different id -1, reset when it hits 0.
approach: Use the Boyer-Moore voting idea: maintain a candidate and a count; matching ids increment, others decrement, and when the count is 0 pick the current id. The guaranteed majority survives.
edgeCases: winner appears only at the end
two ids alternating plus one extra

title: Best streak of profit
statement: A shop records its daily profit (possibly negative) for n days. Choose a streak of one or more consecutive days that has the largest total profit and print that total.
input: One line of n integers.
output: One integer: the maximum total of a non-empty consecutive streak.

examples.why: All days lose money, so the best streak is the single day with -1.

hints: At each day decide: extend the previous streak or start fresh here.
best ending here = max(x, best ending previous + x).
approach: Kadane: keep the best sum of a streak ending at the current day as max(x, previous+x), and track the global maximum. Do not initialise the global maximum to 0 so negative-only input works.

title: Zip two sorted queues
statement: Two queues of customers each list their ticket numbers in ascending order. Merge them into a single ascending list without re-sorting from scratch. Equal numbers from both queues are all kept.
input: Line 1: first sorted list; line 2: second sorted list.
output: The merged list, space separated.
hints: Keep one pointer in each list and always take the smaller head.
When one list runs out, append the rest of the other.
approach: Use two pointers, repeatedly appending the smaller current element and advancing that pointer. Append whatever remains when one list is exhausted.

title: Mirror sentence
statement: A sentence is a mirror if, after dropping every character that is not a letter or digit and ignoring upper/lower case, it reads the same forwards and backwards. Decide whether the given line is a mirror.
input: One line of text (may contain spaces and punctuation).
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: Without spaces: neveroddoreven reads the same both ways.
Cleaned: helloollehx; the trailing x breaks the symmetry.

hints: Filter and lowercase first, or skip junk characters as you go.
Compare from both ends moving inwards.
approach: Use two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lower-cased characters. Any mismatch means false.

title: Flip the headline
statement: Reverse the order of the words in a line of text. Words are separated by one or more spaces, and the input may have extra spaces at the start or end; the output must have words separated by exactly one space and no leading or trailing spaces.
input: One line of text.
output: The words in reverse order.

examples.why: Extra spaces are collapsed after reversing.

hints: Splitting on whitespace discards empty pieces.
Reverse the list of words, then join with one space.
approach: Split the line into words ignoring runs of whitespace, reverse the list, and join with single spaces.

title: The lonely letter
statement: Find the position (0-based) of the first character in a string that occurs exactly once in the whole string. Print -1 if every character repeats.
input: One lowercase string.
output: An integer index or -1.

examples.why: s appears 3 times; w at index 1 appears once.

hints: First count how often each letter appears.
Then scan left to right and return the first letter with count 1.
approach: Count character frequencies in one pass, then scan the string again and return the index of the first character whose count is 1.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (26 letters)

title: Same letters, new order
statement: Two words are anagrams if one can be rearranged into the other using every letter exactly once. Given two lowercase words, say whether they are anagrams.
input: Two lines, one word each.
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: They differ in one letter (t vs c).

hints: Different lengths can never match.
Compare letter counts.
approach: Count letters of the first word, subtract counts of the second, and check all counts are zero (or compare sorted strings).

title: Run-length stamp
statement: Encode a string by replacing each maximal run of the same character with the character followed by the run length. A character that appears once is still written with the count 1.
input: One lowercase string.
output: The encoded string.
hints: Scan with a start index of the current run.
Extend the end while characters match, then emit char and length.
approach: Walk the string, and for each run find its end, append the character and the run length, and jump to the next run.

title: The shared beginning
statement: Given several words, find the longest string that is a prefix of every one of them. Print it, or "-" if the words share no starting letters.
input: One line of space-separated lowercase words.
output: The longest common prefix, or "-".

examples.why: All three begin with "inter"; the next letters are v, n, n, so the prefix stops there.

hints: Start with the first word as a candidate prefix.
Shorten the candidate until each next word starts with it.
approach: Take the first word as the prefix and for every other word trim the prefix until the word starts with it. If it becomes empty, print "-".
complexity: O(total characters) time, O(1) extra space
edgeCases: one word is a prefix of another

title: Secret shift note
statement: Encrypt a message by shifting every letter forward by k places in the alphabet, wrapping from z back to a. Upper-case letters stay upper-case, and non-letters are left untouched.
input: Line 1: the message; line 2: the integer k.
output: The encrypted message.

examples.why: H→K, e→h, ... and the comma and space remain.
x→z, y wraps to a, z wraps to b.

hints: Convert a letter to 0..25, add k, take modulo 26.
Handle upper and lower case with different base characters.
approach: For each letter, subtract the base code (A or a), add k modulo 26, and add the base back. Copy other characters unchanged.

title: Spun label
statement: A label is spun by moving some number of characters from the front to the back (a rotation). Given two strings, decide whether the second could be a spun version of the first (including zero spins).
input: Two lines, one string each.
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: Move "wat" from the front to the back.
Same letters but not a rotation.

hints: A rotation must have the same length.
Every rotation of A appears as a substring of A+A.
approach: If lengths differ answer false. Otherwise check whether B occurs inside A concatenated with itself.
complexity: O(n) time with a linear-time substring search (O(n^2) naive is fine for small n), O(n) space

title: Add the binary bills
statement: Two non-negative numbers are written as binary strings (no leading zeros except the number 0 itself). Add them by hand, digit by digit with a carry, and print the sum as a binary string. The numbers can be too long for built-in integer types.
input: Two lines, each a binary string.
output: The sum in binary.
hints: Walk both strings from the right with a carry.
Append the leftover carry at the end, then reverse.
approach: Two pointers start at the last digits. Sum the digits and carry, record sum%2, carry = sum//2, continue until both strings and the carry are done, then reverse the result.
edgeCases: carry creates a new leading digit

title: Spreadsheet column number
statement: Spreadsheet columns are named A, B, ..., Z, AA, AB, ..., AZ, BA, ... Given a column name made of upper-case letters, print its 1-based column number.
input: One string of capital letters.
output: One integer.
hints: This is like base 26 but letters map to 1..26 instead of 0..25.
Fold left to right: value = value*26 + letter.
approach: Process letters left to right, updating value = value*26 + (letter - 64). The result is the column number.

title: Matching pair of prices
statement: A shopper has a list of item prices and a budget. Exactly one pair of different positions has prices that add up to the budget. Print the two 0-based positions, smaller first.
input: Line 1: n prices; line 2: the budget.
output: Two indices i j with i < j.

examples.why: 1 + 6 = 7 at positions 1 and 3; no other pair works.

hints: For each price you need budget - price to have been seen already.
Store value to index in a hash map as you scan.
approach: Scan left to right, looking up the complement in a hash map of values seen so far. When found, return its stored index and the current one; otherwise store the current value.

title: Repeat visitor
statement: A door logs the badge id of each visitor in order. A repeat visit is suspicious if the same badge id appears at two positions i and j with j - i ≤ k. Print whether any suspicious pair exists.
input: Line 1: n badge ids; line 2: the integer k.
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: The 1s are 3 positions apart, which is ≤ 3.

hints: Only the most recent position of each id matters.
Store last index per id in a hash map.
approach: Keep a map from id to its latest index. On seeing an id again, check whether the distance to the stored index is at most k; update the stored index each time.

title: Anagram clubs
statement: Words that are anagrams of each other form one club. Given a list of lowercase words, count how many clubs there are.
input: One line of space-separated words.
output: One integer: the number of clubs.

examples.in: listen silent enlist google gogole cat act

examples.why: "a" appears twice but is one club, plus "b".

hints: Anagrams share a canonical form.
Use the sorted letters (or a count signature) as the hash key.
approach: Map each word to its sorted-letters signature and put signatures in a set. The size of the set is the number of clubs.
complexity: O(total length * log) time, O(total length) space

title: One-to-one code
statement: Two strings of equal length follow the same code if you can replace each distinct letter of the first by one distinct letter of the second, consistently and one-to-one, to turn the first into the second. Decide whether they do.
input: Two lines, one string each.
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: p→t, a→i, e→l, r→e works in both directions.
o would have to map to both a and r.

hints: You need a mapping and also its inverse.
Reject if either direction conflicts.
approach: Maintain two hash maps, first-to-second and second-to-first. For each aligned pair of characters, any inconsistency in either map means false.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space for a fixed alphabet

title: First to repeat
statement: In a stream of numbers, the first number to repeat is the one whose second occurrence appears earliest in the stream. Print it, or -1 if nothing repeats.
input: One line of n integers.
output: One integer.

examples.why: The second 1 (index 3) comes before the second 3 (index 5).

hints: Which element is repeated is decided at the moment of the second occurrence.
Scan with a set and stop at the first element already in it.
approach: Scan left to right with a hash set. The first element found already in the set is the answer; if the scan ends, print -1.

title: Fans of both bands
statement: Two bands each list the ids of their fans (an id may be listed more than once). Print the ids that appear in both lists, each once, in increasing order, or "-" if there are none.
input: Two lines of integers.
output: Sorted common ids, or "-".
hints: Convert one list to a set.
Collect elements of the other that are in the set, dedupe and sort.
approach: Build sets from both lists, intersect them, and print the sorted result (or "-" if empty).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Top trending tags
statement: Each post carries a numeric tag id. Print the k tag ids that appear most often, most frequent first. If two tags appear equally often, the smaller id comes first.
input: Line 1: n tag ids; line 2: the integer k.
output: k ids separated by spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct ids ≤ n ≤ 10^5

examples.why: 4 and 5 tie at 2; smaller id first; 6 only once.

hints: Count with a hash map.
Sort distinct ids by (-count, id) and take the first k.
approach: Count occurrences with a map, sort the distinct ids with key (-count, id), and output the first k.
complexity: O(n + d log d) time for d distinct ids, O(d) space

title: Biggest pond between walls
statement: Vertical walls stand at positions 0..n-1 with the given heights. Pick two walls and fill the space between them with water; the water level is limited by the shorter wall, and the amount is that height times the distance between the walls (ignore any walls in between). Print the largest amount possible.
input: One line of n wall heights.
output: One integer.
hints: Start with the widest pair of walls.
Move the pointer at the shorter wall inwards; moving the taller one cannot help.
approach: Use two pointers at both ends, computing min(height)*distance each time and then advancing the pointer at the shorter wall, since only a taller wall could improve the area.

title: Mirror with one typo
statement: A word is nearly a mirror if it is a palindrome, or becomes one after deleting at most one character. Decide whether the given word is nearly a mirror.
input: One lowercase string.
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: Deleting c (or b) gives aba (or aca).
No single deletion makes it symmetric.

hints: Walk inwards from both ends until a mismatch.
At the mismatch try skipping the left or the right character and check that the remainder is a palindrome.
approach: Move two pointers inward. On the first mismatch, check whether the substring skipping the left char or the one skipping the right char is a palindrome; if neither, the answer is false.

title: Square the readings
statement: A sensor logs n readings in non-decreasing order, some negative. Print the squares of the readings in non-decreasing order, without simply squaring and sorting from scratch.
input: One line of n sorted integers.
output: The sorted squares.
hints: The largest square is at one of the two ends.
Fill the output from the back, taking the larger absolute value of the two ends each time.
approach: Place pointers at both ends. The larger absolute value yields the largest remaining square; write it at the end of the output and move that pointer inward.

title: Three-flag sort
statement: A row of flags is coloured 0 (red), 1 (white) or 2 (blue). Reorder them so all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s, in a single pass and without counting or a library sort.
input: One line of n values from {0,1,2}.
output: The reordered row.
hints: Keep three regions: zeros at the front, twos at the back, unknown in the middle.
Swap a 0 to the front pointer, a 2 to the back pointer, and just advance on a 1.
approach: Use pointers lo, mid, hi. If a[mid] is 0 swap with lo and advance both; if 1 advance mid; if 2 swap with hi and shrink hi (do not advance mid).

title: Cheap duos
statement: A shop sells n items. A duo is a pair of different items; count the duos whose total price is strictly less than a given budget. The input order is arbitrary.
input: Line 1: n prices; line 2: the budget.
output: One integer.

examples.why: (1,3) and (1,5); (1,7) equals 8 which is not less.

hints: Sort the prices first.
If a[l]+a[r] < budget, then a[l] pairs with every element from l+1 to r.
approach: Sort, then use pointers l and r. When a[l]+a[r] is under the budget, add r-l pairs and advance l; otherwise decrement r.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Hidden word
statement: A word is hidden in a longer text if you can find all its letters in the text in the same order, though not necessarily next to each other. Decide whether the first string is hidden in the second.
input: Line 1: the word; line 2: the text.
output: "true" or "false".

examples.why: a, c, e appear in order in abcde.
After a and e, no c remains.

hints: Use one pointer on the word and one on the text.
Advance the word pointer only when letters match.
approach: Scan the text; each time the current text letter equals the next needed letter of the word, advance the word pointer. The word is hidden if the pointer reaches its end.

title: Mirror the vowels
statement: In a word, keep every consonant where it is, but reverse the order of the vowels (a, e, i, o, u, in either case). Print the new word; letter case moves with each letter.
input: One word of letters.
output: The transformed word.

examples.why: The vowels e and o swap.
Vowels A, o, i become i, o, A in their slots.

hints: Use pointers from both ends, each hunting for the next vowel.
Swap when both stand on vowels.
approach: Two pointers move inward, skipping non-vowels; when both point at vowels, swap them and move both. Stop when they cross.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for a char array

title: Longest hill
statement: A hill in a list of altitudes is a stretch of at least 3 values that strictly rises to a single peak and then strictly falls. Print the length of the longest hill, or 0 if there is none.
input: One line of n altitudes.
output: One integer.
hints: Find each peak (greater than both neighbours).
From each peak extend left while rising and right while falling.
approach: For each index that is a strict peak, expand left while values strictly decrease going left and right while they strictly decrease going right. The hill length is right - left + 1; skip ahead past the right end.

title: Best k-day stretch
statement: A farm stand records daily sales for n days. Find the largest total sales over any k consecutive days.
input: Line 1: n daily sales; line 2: k.
output: One integer.
hints: Compute the first window sum, then slide.
Add the entering value, subtract the leaving one.
approach: Compute the sum of the first k values, then slide one position at a time adding the new element and removing the oldest, tracking the maximum.

title: Stretch with no repeats
statement: Find the length of the longest contiguous piece of a string in which no character appears twice.
input: One string.
output: One integer.
hints: Maintain a window [l, r] with all-distinct characters.
Remember the last index of each character so l can jump.
approach: Expand r over the string; when s[r] was last seen inside the window, move l to just after that earlier occurrence. Record the best r-l+1.

title: Warm enough windows
statement: Given daily temperatures, count the windows of exactly k consecutive days whose average temperature is at least a threshold t.
input: Line 1: n temperatures; line 2: k; line 3: t.
output: One integer.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10^5; values and t are integers, |values| ≤ 10^4
hints: Avoid floating point: compare window sum with t*k.
Update the sum incrementally.
approach: Maintain the window sum and compare it with t*k at each position; each slide adds one value and removes one.

title: Vowel-heavy window
statement: Among all substrings of length exactly k of a lowercase string, find the largest number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) that any one of them contains.
input: Line 1: the string; line 2: k.
output: One integer.
hints: Keep a running count of vowels in the window.
Add 1 for an entering vowel and subtract 1 for a leaving vowel.
approach: Count vowels in the first k characters, then slide: add the entering character if it is a vowel and subtract the leaving one. Track the maximum.

title: Crowd favourites first
statement: Reorder a list of song ids so that ids that occur more often come first. Equal ids stay grouped together, and ids with the same count are ordered by smaller id first.
input: One line of n integers.
output: The reordered list.

examples.why: 3 and 5 tie at 2, so 3 goes first; 1 last.

hints: Count first, then sort with a custom key.
Key = (-count, value).
approach: Count the occurrences, then sort the list using the key (-count[x], x). Equal values end up adjacent because they share the same key.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Kth fastest lap
statement: Lap scores are recorded for a race, where a higher score is better. Print the k-th highest score, counting duplicates as separate laps (so two equal best scores are 1st and 2nd).
input: Line 1: n scores; line 2: k.
output: One integer.
hints: Sort in descending order and index k-1.
For large n a heap or quickselect avoids the full sort.
approach: Sort the scores in descending order and return the element at index k-1. A min-heap of size k would give O(n log k).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Fan index
statement: An author has papers with the given citation counts. Their index is the largest h such that at least h of their papers have at least h citations each. Print h.
input: One line of n citation counts.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Four papers have at least 4 citations (10, 8, 5, 4).

hints: Sort in descending order.
Find the last position k (1-based) with value ≥ k.
approach: Sort descending. The answer is the largest k such that the k-th value is at least k.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: House alphabet order
statement: A company ranks letters by its own order string (no repeats). Sort a text by that ranking; letters missing from the order string go after all ranked letters, keeping their original relative order.
input: Line 1: the order string; line 2: the text.
output: The sorted text.

examples.why: z, y, then unranked x's in original order.

hints: Map each ranked letter to its position.
Use a stable sort with unranked letters mapped to a large rank.
approach: Build a rank map from the order string, give unknown letters rank len(order), and do a stable sort of the text by rank.
complexity: O(n log n) time (or O(n + 26) with counting), O(n) space

title: Closest neighbours
statement: Among a list of integers (values may repeat), find the smallest absolute difference between any two elements, and how many adjacent pairs in sorted order achieve it. Print both numbers.
input: One line of n integers.
output: Two integers: the minimum difference and the number of sorted-adjacent pairs achieving it.

examples.why: Sorted 10 10 20: only the first gap is 0.

hints: The smallest difference is always between sorted neighbours.
Compute all neighbour gaps after sorting.
approach: Sort the array, compute the gaps between consecutive elements, take their minimum and count how many gaps equal it.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Podium ranks
statement: Contestants have distinct scores. Print each contestant's rank in the original order, where rank 1 is the highest score.
input: One line of n distinct integers.
output: n ranks in input order.
hints: Sort the scores to learn each rank.
Store rank by score in a map, then read it back in input order.
approach: Sort scores descending, assign rank = position + 1 in a map from score to rank, then output the rank for each original score.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Cheapest matchup
statement: You have two lists of equal length: hours of work and hourly rates. Pair each hours value with exactly one rate (each used once, any pairing allowed) so that the sum of hours*rate is as small as possible. Print that minimum.
input: Two lines of n positive integers.
output: One integer.

examples.why: All rates equal, so the sum is (1+2)*3.

hints: Pair the largest with the smallest.
Sort one list ascending and the other descending.
approach: By the rearrangement inequality the minimum sum of products pairs the smallest of one list with the largest of the other. Sort one ascending, the other descending, and sum the products.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Canoe pairs
statement: Hikers with the given weights must cross a river in canoes. Each canoe carries at most two people and a total weight of at most cap (every hiker alone is guaranteed to fit). Print the smallest number of canoes needed.
input: Line 1: n weights; line 2: cap.
output: One integer.
hints: Sort the weights.
Try to pair the heaviest with the lightest; if they do not fit, the heaviest goes alone.
approach: Sort, then use two pointers: always send the heaviest hiker; if the lightest also fits, send them together and advance the left pointer. Count canoes.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Where does it go
statement: A sorted list of distinct bib numbers is given. For a new number, print the index where it is, or the index where it would be inserted to keep the list sorted.
input: Line 1: sorted distinct integers; line 2: the query.
output: One integer index.

examples.why: 5 would sit between 4 and 6, at index 2.
Larger than all, so goes at the end (index 4).

hints: Search for the first position whose value is ≥ the query.
Keep lo and hi, and move hi to mid when a[mid] ≥ query.
approach: Binary search for the lower bound: lo=0, hi=n; while lo<hi take mid, if a[mid] < q set lo=mid+1 else hi=mid. Return lo.

title: First and last sighting
statement: A sorted list may repeat values. For a given target, print the index of its first and last occurrence, or "-1 -1" if it is absent.
input: Line 1: sorted integers; line 2: target.
output: Two integers.
hints: Run one binary search for the left edge and one for the right edge.
Right edge = (first index greater than target) - 1.
approach: Use lower bound for the first index with value ≥ t and upper bound for the first index with value > t. If they are equal the target is absent; otherwise answer (lower, upper-1).

title: Whole square root
statement: Print the largest integer r such that r*r ≤ n, without using floating-point square root.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer.
hints: The predicate r*r ≤ n is true for small r and false for large r.
Binary search for the last r where it is true.
approach: Binary search r in [0, n], testing mid*mid ≤ n, keeping the largest passing value. Use an upper-mid to avoid an infinite loop.

title: Coldest point on the dial
statement: A sorted list of distinct numbers was rotated at an unknown point. Print the smallest number in it in logarithmic time.
input: One line of the rotated list.
output: One integer.

examples.why: The drop from 6 to 1 marks the start.
Not rotated, so the first is the minimum.

hints: Compare a[mid] with a[hi].
If a[mid] > a[hi] the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or left.
approach: Binary search with lo, hi: if a[mid] > a[hi] set lo=mid+1, else set hi=mid. When lo equals hi that element is the minimum.

title: Next letter up
statement: Letters in a sorted list are used as labels. Given a target letter, print the smallest label that is strictly greater than it; if none is, wrap around and print the first label.
input: Line 1: sorted lowercase letters separated by spaces; line 2: target letter.
output: One letter.

examples.why: f is the first letter after c.
Nothing is greater than z, so wrap to c.

hints: This is an upper-bound search.
If the index reaches n, use index 0.
approach: Find the first index with letter > target using binary search (upper bound) and return that letter, using index modulo n to handle the wrap.

title: Cube for the crate
statement: A cubic box with integer side x holds x*x*x units. Given a volume n, find the smallest integer side x whose box holds at least n units.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer.
hints: The predicate x^3 ≥ n is false then true as x grows.
Search for the first x where it becomes true.
approach: Binary search x in [0, n] for the first value with x^3 ≥ n: if mid^3 ≥ n shrink the right bound to mid, else move the left bound past mid.

title: Range totals
statement: A bakery logs how many loaves it sold each day. Answer q questions of the form "how many loaves were sold from day l through day r (inclusive, 0-based)?" quickly.
input: Line 1: n daily counts; line 2: q; then q lines each with l and r.
output: q lines, one total each.
hints: Precompute prefix[i] = sum of the first i items.
Answer = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
approach: Build a prefix array with prefix[0]=0 and prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+a[i]. Each query is prefix[r+1]-prefix[l] in constant time.

title: The balance point
statement: On a seesaw, weights are placed at positions 0..n-1. A balance point is a position whose left side total equals its right side total (the weight at the point itself is not counted on either side, and an empty side counts as 0). Print the leftmost balance point, or -1.
input: One line of n integers.
output: An index or -1.
hints: Compute the total sum once.
Walk left to right keeping the left sum; the right sum is total - left - current.
approach: Compute the total, then iterate with a running left sum. At index i the right sum is total - left - a[i]; return the first i where left equals right.

title: First day in the red
statement: An account starts at 0. Each day a deposit (positive) or withdrawal (negative) is applied. Print the 1-based number of the first day after which the balance is below zero, or -1 if it never goes below zero.
input: One line of n integers.
output: An integer day or -1.
hints: Keep a running balance.
Stop at the first time it is below 0.
approach: Maintain the running sum while scanning; return the 1-based index the first time it drops below zero, otherwise -1.

title: Plot of land totals
statement: A farm is a grid of plots, each with a crop yield. Answer q queries asking for the total yield inside a rectangle given by its top-left and bottom-right plots (0-based, inclusive).
input: Line 1: rows and columns; then the grid rows; then q; then q lines "r1 c1 r2 c2".
output: q lines, one total each.
hints: Build a 2D prefix table P where P[i][j] is the sum of the top-left i by j block.
Inclusion-exclusion: whole - top strip - left strip + overlap.

title: Bulk price changes
statement: A catalogue lists item prices. You receive q updates, each adding an amount v to every price in a range l..r (inclusive, 0-based). Apply all updates and print the final prices, doing it faster than touching every item for every update.
input: Line 1: n prices; line 2: q; then q lines "l r v".
output: The final prices.
hints: Record +v at l and -v at r+1 in a difference array.
A running sum of the difference array gives each item's total change.
approach: Keep a difference array d: add v to d[l] and subtract v from d[r+1]. After all updates, take the prefix sum of d and add it to the original prices.

title: Safe starting fuel
statement: A rover starts with some integer amount of fuel and then passes through a series of stations; each changes the fuel by the given amount (positive adds, negative uses). The fuel must stay at least 1 after every station. Find the smallest starting fuel (a positive integer) that works.
input: One line of n integers.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Running changes: 2, -3, -2, -3, 0 — lowest is -3, so start with 4.
The running total never dips below 0.

hints: Look at the lowest prefix sum.
Start + lowest prefix must be ≥ 1.
approach: Compute the minimum prefix sum m (with 0 allowed as the starting value). The start must satisfy start + m ≥ 1, so the answer is 1 - m.

title: Fair cut points
statement: Cut a row of values into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part at one of the n-1 gaps. Count the cuts where the left part's sum is at least the right part's sum.
input: One line of n integers (n ≥ 2).
output: One integer.

examples.why: Total is 6: cuts give 3 vs 3 (ok), 4 vs 2 (ok), 2 vs 4 (not ok).

hints: Right sum = total - left sum.
Scan the cut positions with a running left sum.
approach: Compute the total, then for each cut position 1..n-1 maintain the left sum and compare with total - left, counting cuts where left ≥ right.

title: Merge the bookings
statement: A hall has several bookings, each a closed interval [start, end] and not in any particular order. Bookings that overlap or touch (share an endpoint) should be merged into one. Print the merged bookings in increasing order, one per line.
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end".
output: The merged intervals, one "start end" per line.
hints: Sort by start.
Extend the last merged interval if the next start is ≤ its end; else begin a new one.
approach: Sort intervals by start. Keep a result list; for each interval, if it starts at or before the end of the last result, extend that end with the max, otherwise append it.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: A day with no clashes
statement: A person has meetings given as [start, end) — a meeting ending at 10 and another starting at 10 do not clash. Decide whether they can attend all of them.
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end".
output: "true" or "false".
hints: Sort by start time.
Only neighbouring meetings can clash after sorting.
approach: Sort by start and check that every meeting starts no earlier than the previous one ends; any violation means false.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Overlapping shifts
statement: Two employees each have a sorted list of non-overlapping closed work intervals. Print every interval during which both are working, in order, one per line, or "-" if they never overlap.
input: Line 1: n; n lines; then m; m lines.
output: The intersections, one "start end" per line, or "-".
hints: Use one pointer in each list.
The overlap of two intervals is [max starts, min ends] if that is valid.
approach: Walk both lists with two pointers. Compute lo = max of starts and hi = min of ends; if lo ≤ hi record it. Then advance the pointer whose interval ends first.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space

title: Total painted length
statement: A painter paints several segments of a long wall, each a closed range [start, end] on a number line, possibly overlapping. Print the total length of wall that ends up painted at least once (a segment [a, b] has length b - a).
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end".
output: One integer.

examples.why: A single point has no length.

hints: Overlapping parts must not be counted twice.
Merge the intervals first, then add up lengths.
approach: Sort and merge overlapping intervals, then sum end - start of each merged interval.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Free time finder
statement: A day runs from time 0 to time T. Several busy intervals may overlap each other. Print the free intervals within [0, T] (gaps of positive length), in order, one per line, or "-" if there are none.
input: Line 1: T; line 2: n; then n lines "start end".
output: Free intervals, one per line, or "-".

examples.why: Gaps before, between and after the busy blocks.

hints: Sort and merge busy intervals first.
Walk from time 0, recording the gap before each busy block, and finally the gap to T.
approach: Merge the busy intervals, then track a cursor starting at 0: a merged interval starting after the cursor creates a free gap; move the cursor to its end. Add a final gap if the cursor is before T.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Not swallowed
statement: You have distinct closed ranges [a, b]. A range is swallowed if another range [c, d] satisfies c ≤ a and b ≤ d. Count the ranges that are not swallowed by any other.
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end" (all ranges distinct).
output: One integer.

examples.why: [3,6] sits inside [2,8]; the other two survive.

hints: Sort by start ascending, and by end descending when starts tie.
A range is swallowed if its end does not exceed the largest end seen so far.
approach: Sort by start ascending, end descending. Scan keeping the maximum end so far; a range whose end is greater than that maximum is new (count it), otherwise it is swallowed.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Balanced crate labels
statement: A warehouse labels each crate stack with brackets: round, square and curly. A label is valid if every opener is closed by the same kind of closer, in the right nesting order. Decide whether a given label string is valid.
input: One line containing only the characters ()[]{}.
output: true or false.

examples.why: Every pair closes in the correct nesting order.
The ] arrives while the most recent open bracket is (, so the nesting is broken.

hints: Whenever you see an opener, you will need to remember it until its closer shows up.
Keep openers on a stack; on a closer, the top of the stack must be its partner. At the end the stack must be empty.
approach: Push each opener on a stack. For each closer, pop and check it matches, failing on an empty stack or mismatch. Valid only if the stack is empty at the end.

title: Typing with backspace
statement: A note app records keystrokes: letters are typed, and the character # is a backspace that deletes the previous letter (doing nothing on empty text). Given the keystroke string, print the text that ends up on screen.
input: One line of lowercase letters and #.
output: The final text, or the word EMPTY if nothing remains.

examples.why: ab, then abd, then ab, then a, then ae.
Backspaces on empty text do nothing, and the last # erases x.

hints: Think of the text as something where only the last character can be removed.
Use a list as a stack: push letters, pop on # if non-empty.
approach: Scan once, pushing letters on a stack and popping on #. Join the stack at the end.

title: Postfix calculator
statement: A retro calculator takes expressions in postfix form: operands first, then the operator. Tokens are integers and the operators +, - and *. Evaluate the expression.
input: One line of space-separated tokens forming a valid postfix expression.
output: The integer result.
constraints: 1 ≤ tokens ≤ 10^4; every intermediate value fits in 64-bit
hints: When an operator appears, which two values does it use?
Push numbers; on an operator pop b then a and push a op b. Order matters for subtraction.
approach: Scan the tokens with a stack. Numbers are pushed; for an operator pop the right operand then the left, apply it and push the result. The remaining item is the answer.

title: Strip the twin letters
statement: Repeatedly delete any two equal letters that sit next to each other until no such pair remains. Print the final string; removals can create new neighbouring pairs.
input: One line of lowercase letters.
output: The reduced string, or EMPTY if nothing is left.

examples.why: bb goes first giving aaca, then aa goes, leaving ca.
xx goes, then the two z letters meet and go, leaving ay.

hints: After removing a pair, which two letters become neighbours?
A stack gives you the previous surviving letter instantly: if it equals the new letter, pop.
approach: Process letters left to right with a stack. If the top equals the current letter, pop; otherwise push. The stack content is the answer.
edgeCases: Three equal letters in a row

title: Train shunting check
statement: Distinct wagons arrive on a single siding in a known order and can be pushed onto a dead-end track; the wagon at the end may be pulled out at any time. Given the arrival order and a target departure order, decide whether the target can be produced.
input: Two lines of distinct integers of equal length: arrival order, then desired departure order.
output: true or false.

examples.why: After pulling 4,3,5 the end wagon is 2, but 1 is wanted.

hints: Simulate the track directly.
Push arrivals one by one and pull while the end wagon equals the next desired wagon.
approach: Push each arriving wagon on a stack and, after every push, pop while the top equals the next wagon of the target. The order is possible iff all target wagons were popped.

title: Price streak
statement: A trader records a share price each day. For every day, count how many consecutive days ending on that day (including itself) had a price less than or equal to that day's price.
input: One line of positive integers, the daily prices.
output: One line with the streak length for each day.

examples.why: On day 6 (45) the streak covers 45,20,35,30,40 so 5; the 60 beats everything, giving 7.
Equal prices count, so streaks grow 1 2 3 4.

hints: Scanning left each time is O(n^2).
Keep a stack of indices with strictly greater prices; the streak is the distance to the top.
approach: Maintain a stack of indices with decreasing prices. For day i pop all indices with price ≤ current, then the streak is i minus the new top index (or i+1 if empty).

title: Patch the parentheses
statement: A string of round brackets may be unbalanced. You may insert brackets anywhere. Find the minimum number of insertions needed so that every opener is matched with a later closer.
input: One line containing only ( and ).
output: The minimum number of insertions.

examples.why: The second ) has no opener and the last ( has no closer: 2 insertions.
One opener is never closed: 1 insertion.

hints: Track how many openers are still waiting.
On a closer with nothing waiting you must add an opener; leftover waiting openers need closers.
approach: Scan with a counter of open brackets. A closer with zero open increases the insertion count; otherwise it decrements. The answer is insertions plus the leftover open count.

title: Game score keeper
statement: A game logs events: a number means you scored that many points, C cancels the previous valid score, D scores double the previous valid score, and + scores the sum of the previous two valid scores. Compute the total of all valid scores at the end.
input: One line of space-separated tokens.
output: The total score.

examples.why: Scores 5, 2; C drops 2; D adds 10; + adds 15. Total 5+10+15=30.

hints: You only ever look at or remove the most recent scores.
Keep valid scores on a stack and sum it at the end.
approach: Process tokens with a stack of valid scores: C pops, D pushes twice the top, + pushes the sum of the top two, numbers are pushed. Sum the stack.

title: Hot potato circle
statement: n kids numbered 1..n stand in a circle and the potato starts with kid 1, who counts as 1. Counting k kids around the circle, the kid who gets count k leaves, and counting restarts from the next kid. Print the number of the last kid standing.
input: One line with integers n and k.
output: The number of the last remaining kid.

examples.why: Kids leave in the order 2, 4, 1, 5; kid 3 remains.

hints: Model the circle as a queue and simulate.
Move k-1 kids from the front to the back, then remove the front kid.
approach: Put 1..n in a deque. Repeat: rotate k-1 kids from front to back, then pop the front. When one remains it is the answer. Simulation costs O(nk); a modulo shortcut can skip the rotations.
complexity: O(n*k) time with a plain queue, O(n) space

title: Recent pings
statement: A server logs ping timestamps in milliseconds, in non-decreasing order. After each ping, report how many pings (including this one) arrived in the last 3000 ms, meaning timestamps in [t-3000, t].
input: One line of non-decreasing integers.
output: One line with the count after each ping.

examples.why: At 3001 the window [1,3001] holds 3 pings; at 3002 the window [2,3002] has 100, 3001, 3002.
500 expires before 4000; at 7500 only 4500 and 7500 remain.

hints: Old pings never become relevant again.
Keep a queue; drop from the front while the front is older than t-3000.
approach: Append each timestamp to a queue and pop from the front while it is older than t-3000. The queue length is the answer.

title: Card reveal trick
statement: A magician deals a pile: reveal the top card, then move the next top card to the bottom without showing it, and repeat until the pile is gone. The last remaining card is simply revealed. Given the pile from top to bottom, list the cards in reveal order.
input: One line of integers, the pile top to bottom.
output: The reveal order on one line.
hints: A queue models a pile with a top and a bottom.
Pop front to output, then pop front again and push it to the back, if anything remains.
approach: Use a deque. Loop: pop the front into the output, and if cards remain, pop the next front and append it to the back.

title: Binary ticket numbers
statement: A raffle numbers its tickets with the binary numbers 1, 10, 11, 100, ... in increasing order. Generate the first n ticket numbers as strings, using a queue rather than converting integers.
input: One line with the integer n.
output: The first n binary strings separated by spaces.
hints: Each number x spawns the next ones x0 and x1.
Start the queue with 1; pop x, output it, push x+'0' then x+'1'.
approach: Seed a queue with '1'. Repeat n times: pop the front, record it, and enqueue the front with '0' appended and then '1' appended. This yields numbers in increasing order.
complexity: O(n) strings generated (O(n log n) characters)

title: First fresh letter
statement: Letters arrive one at a time. After each arrival, report the first letter in the stream so far that has appeared exactly once, or # if there is none.
input: One line of lowercase letters.
output: A string of the same length with the answer after each arrival.

examples.why: After a: a; after aa: none; after aab: b; after aabc: b.
x, x, then y once x repeats, then # when both repeat. Result xxy#.

hints: The answer can only move forward in arrival order.
Queue candidates in arrival order with a count table; discard the front while its count exceeds 1.
approach: Keep a count per letter and a queue of letters in arrival order. After each arrival, pop front letters whose count is above 1; the front (if any) is the answer.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) alphabet space plus queue

title: Queue from two stacks
statement: Build a first-in-first-out queue using only two stacks. Process commands push x, pop and peek; pop and peek print the front value, or -1 if the queue is empty, and pop also removes it.
input: One line of commands separated by commas.
output: The printed values for pop and peek commands, space-separated.

examples.why: peek 1, pop 1, then pop 2 and pop 3 in arrival order: 1 1 2 3.
pop on empty gives -1, then 5, then -1.

hints: One stack takes new items; the other serves the front.
Only refill the out-stack when it is empty, moving everything from the in-stack.
approach: Use an in-stack for pushes and an out-stack for pops. When the out-stack is empty, move all items from the in-stack; the out-stack top is then the queue front. Each item moves at most once.
complexity: Amortised O(1) per operation, O(n) space

title: Ticket line timing
statement: People stand in a line, and person i wants t[i] tickets. Each second the person at the front buys exactly one ticket; if they still want more they go to the back, otherwise they leave. Find how many seconds pass until person k has bought all their tickets.
input: Line 1: the wishes t. Line 2: the index k (0-based).
output: The number of seconds until person k is done.

examples.why: Seconds: p0,p1,p2,p0,p1,p2 - person 2 finishes at second 6.
p0,p1,p2 buy first, then p0 buys alone for 4 more seconds: 7.

hints: A direct simulation with a queue works for these limits.
Faster: person i contributes min(t[i], t[k]) seconds if i ≤ k, otherwise min(t[i], t[k]-1).
approach: Simulate with a queue of (index, remaining) until person k reaches zero. Or compute the sum of per-person contributions directly in O(n).
complexity: O(n) with the formula; O(n * max t) for simulation

title: Reverse the front of the queue
statement: Given a queue of integers and a number k, reverse the order of the first k elements while keeping the rest in their original order. Use queue operations (and perhaps one stack) in your solution.
input: Line 1: the queue front to back. Line 2: k.
output: The resulting queue, front to back.
hints: A stack reverses whatever you pour into it.
Pop k items into a stack, push them back to the queue, then rotate the remaining n-k items behind them.
approach: Dequeue the first k elements onto a stack, then enqueue them back from the stack (reversed). Finally dequeue and re-enqueue the remaining n-k elements so they follow the reversed block.

title: Single window total wait
statement: A service desk has one window and serves customers in arrival order. Customer i arrives at time a[i] (non-decreasing) and needs d[i] minutes; service starts as soon as the window is free and the customer has arrived. Compute the sum of all waiting times (service start minus arrival).
input: Line 1: arrival times. Line 2: service durations.
output: The total waiting time.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5; times up to 10^9; total fits in 64-bit

examples.why: Customer 2 starts at 5 (waits 4), customer 3 starts at 8 (waits 6): total 10.
The window is free when each customer arrives: total 0.

hints: Track when the window next becomes free.
Start = max(free time, arrival); wait += start - arrival; free = start + duration.
approach: Keep a variable for the time the window becomes free. For each customer in order compute the start time as max(free, arrival), add the wait, and update the free time.

title: Reverse the chain
statement: A singly linked list of integers is given by its values from head to tail. Reverse the list by re-pointing the links, and print the values of the new list from head to tail.
input: One line of integers, or EMPTY.
output: The reversed list, or EMPTY.
hints: Walk once, remembering where you came from.
Keep prev, cur and next pointers; set cur.next = prev, then advance all three.
approach: Iterate with three pointers: save next, point current's link backwards to prev, then move prev and current forward. The final prev is the new head.

title: Middle onward
statement: Given a singly linked list, find its middle node and print the list from that node to the tail. If there are two middle nodes, use the second one. Try to do it in a single pass over the list.
input: One line of integers (at least one).
output: Values from the middle node to the end.

examples.why: The middle node holds 3, so print 3 4 5.
Two middles; take the second one: 3 4.

hints: Could two walkers moving at different speeds meet your goal?
Move slow one step and fast two steps; when fast runs off the end, slow is at the middle.
approach: Use slow and fast pointers starting at the head. Advance fast by two and slow by one while fast and fast.next exist. Slow ends on the second middle.

title: Loop detector
statement: A linked list's last node may point back to an earlier node, forming a loop. You are told the node values and the 0-based index that the tail links back to (-1 means it ends normally). Decide whether the list contains a loop, using an approach that would work without being told the index.
input: Line 1: the node values. Line 2: the index the tail links to, or -1.
output: true or false.

examples.why: The tail links back to the node at index 1, so there is a loop.

hints: If you walk forever, what does that say about the list?
Use a slow pointer (1 step) and a fast pointer (2 steps); they meet iff there is a loop.
approach: Run Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one node, fast moves two. If fast reaches null there is no loop; if they ever point to the same node, there is a loop.

title: Zip two sorted chains
statement: Two linked lists are each sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge them into one sorted list by relinking nodes, and print the values of the merged list.
input: Two lines, each a sorted list of integers or EMPTY.
output: The merged sorted list, or EMPTY.

examples.why: Taking the smaller head each time gives 1 2 3 4 9 10.
With one list empty the other is the answer.

hints: Compare the two current heads.
Use a dummy head node and append the smaller head each step; attach the leftover list at the end.
approach: Create a dummy node and a tail pointer. While both lists have nodes, link the smaller one and advance it. Append whichever list remains and return dummy.next.

title: Drop the nth from the end
statement: Remove the n-th node counted from the tail of a linked list (the last node is n=1) and print the resulting list. Aim for a single pass over the list.
input: Line 1: the list. Line 2: n.
output: The list after removal, or EMPTY.

examples.why: The second from the end is 4; removing it leaves 1 2 3 5.
Removing the only node leaves EMPTY.

hints: You do not know the length in advance, but two pointers can keep a fixed gap.
Move a lead pointer n steps ahead, then move both until lead hits the end; the trailing pointer is just before the target (use a dummy head).
approach: Put a dummy node before the head. Advance a lead pointer n steps, then move lead and trail together until lead is at the last node. Trail.next is the node to remove.

title: Dedupe a sorted chain
statement: In a sorted singly linked list some values appear several times. Remove the extra copies so each value appears once, keeping the first occurrence, and print the result.
input: One line of non-decreasing integers, or EMPTY.
output: The deduplicated list.

examples.why: All copies collapse into one node: 4.

hints: Duplicates are always next to each other.
If cur.val == cur.next.val, skip the next node; otherwise advance.
approach: Walk with one pointer. While the next node has the same value, bypass it by relinking cur.next to cur.next.next; otherwise move on.

title: Mirror chain
statement: Decide whether the values of a singly linked list read the same from head to tail as from tail to head. Try to avoid using O(n) extra memory.
input: One line of integers (at least one).
output: true or false.
hints: Copying to an array works but costs memory.
Find the middle, reverse the second half in place, then compare the halves node by node.
approach: Use slow/fast pointers to find the middle, reverse the second half in place, and compare it with the first half. Optionally restore the list afterwards.

title: Odd-even regroup
statement: Regroup a linked list so all nodes in odd positions (1st, 3rd, ...) come first, followed by all nodes in even positions, keeping the original relative order inside each group. Positions refer to node order, not values.
input: One line of integers, or EMPTY.
output: The regrouped list.
hints: Build two chains as you walk.
Keep odd and even tails; alternately append nodes, then link the odd chain's tail to the even chain's head.
approach: Walk the list, relinking alternate nodes to an odd chain and an even chain. At the end connect the odd tail to the even head.

title: Tallest branch
statement: A family tree is stored as a binary tree. Count the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: A single integer, the maximum depth.
hints: Think recursively: how does a node's height relate to its children's?
depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), and an empty tree has depth 0.
approach: Recursively compute 1 + max of the children's depths, returning 0 for a missing node. A BFS counting levels works equally well.

title: Floor by floor
statement: Print the nodes of a binary tree level by level, from the root downwards and left to right within each level. Separate levels with ' | '.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: Levels on one line, levels separated by ' | ', values by spaces.

examples.why: A right-leaning chain: one node per level.

hints: Process all nodes of one depth before moving on.
Use a queue; for each level, take the current queue size and process exactly that many nodes.
approach: BFS with a queue. At each round remember the queue length, pop that many nodes into the level's list, and enqueue their children.
complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space (w = max width)

title: Mirror-image tree
statement: Decide whether a binary tree is symmetric around its centre: the left subtree must be the mirror image of the right subtree, in both shape and values. Decide whether the given tree is symmetric.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: true or false.

examples.why: Both children have only a right child, which is not a mirror.

hints: Compare two subtrees at once rather than one.
isMirror(a,b): both empty is true; values equal and isMirror(a.left,b.right) and isMirror(a.right,b.left).
approach: Recursively test a pair of nodes: both null is true, one null is false, otherwise values must match and the outer pair and inner pair must also mirror. Start with the root's two children.

title: Flip the tree
statement: Swap the left and right children of every node in a binary tree, producing its mirror image. Print the flipped tree in the same level-order format.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: The flipped tree in level-order with null markers (trailing nulls omitted).

examples.why: Root children swap to 3 2, and 2's children swap to 5 4: 1 3 2 null null 5 4.
The right child 8 (with left child 7) moves to the left, and 7 becomes a right child.

hints: Every node does the same small job.
Recurse into both children, then swap them (or swap first, then recurse).
approach: Do a DFS; at each node swap its two children and recurse into both. A BFS with a queue gives the same result.

title: Trail total
statement: Each node of a binary tree holds a toll. Determine whether some path that starts at the root and ends at a leaf has tolls adding up exactly to a target value.
input: Line 1: the tree in level-order with null. Line 2: the target integer.
output: true or false.

examples.why: Root-to-leaf sums are 18, 22 and 22, so 20 is impossible.

hints: Subtract each node's value from the target as you go down.
At a leaf, check whether the remaining target equals the leaf's value.
approach: DFS with a remaining target. At a leaf, return remaining == value. Otherwise return true if either child can reach target - value.
edgeCases: Path must end at a leaf, not any node

title: Right edge view
statement: Stand to the right of a binary tree and look at it. List, from top to bottom, the value of the node you see at each depth - the rightmost node of every level.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: The visible values from top to bottom.

examples.why: A left chain is fully visible: 1 2 3.

hints: Each level contributes one value.
Do a level-order traversal and keep the last node of each level.
approach: BFS by levels, recording the last node processed at each level. DFS visiting right children first and recording the first node seen at each new depth also works.
edgeCases: Deeper left branch hidden shows up lower

title: Left leaf sum
statement: In a binary tree, a left leaf is a node with no children that is the left child of its parent. Add up the values of all left leaves.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: The sum of left-leaf values (0 if none).

examples.why: Left leaves are 2 (child of 4) and 5 (child of 6): total 7.
The root is not a left child, so 0.

hints: You need to know how a node relates to its parent.
Pass a flag isLeft down the recursion; add the value when a leaf has the flag set.
approach: DFS with a boolean telling whether the node is a left child. A leaf with the flag adds its value; internal nodes sum the results from their children.
edgeCases: Leaf that is a right child

title: Twin trees
statement: Two binary trees are twins if they have exactly the same shape and the same value in every matching position. Decide whether the two given trees are twins.
input: Two lines, each a binary tree in level-order with null.
output: true or false.

examples.why: The same values but 2 is a left child in one and a right child in the other.

hints: Compare the two trees node by node in the same position.
same(a,b): both null true; one null false; equal values and same(a.left,b.left) and same(a.right,b.right).
approach: Recurse in lockstep on both trees. A mismatch in presence or value returns false; otherwise both subtree pairs must match.

title: How deep is it
statement: Build a binary search tree by inserting values in the order given. Then report the depth of a query value (the root has depth 0), or -1 if the value is not in the tree.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: the query value.
output: The depth of the value, or -1.

examples.why: 7 is not stored in the tree.

hints: Use the BST ordering to decide where to go next.
Starting at the root, go left if the query is smaller, right if larger, counting steps until you find it or fall off.
approach: Insert values with the standard BST rule, then search from the root while counting steps; return -1 if you reach a missing child.

title: k-th smallest key
statement: Insert the given values into a binary search tree and report the k-th smallest value stored (k = 1 is the minimum). Use the BST's structure rather than sorting the raw input.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: k.
output: The k-th smallest value.
hints: What traversal of a BST produces sorted order?
Do an in-order traversal and stop after visiting k nodes.
approach: Perform an iterative in-order traversal with a stack, counting visited nodes, and return the value when the counter reaches k.

title: Range total
statement: A BST stores sales figures. Given a low and a high bound, compute the sum of all stored values that lie in the closed range [low, high]. Skip subtrees that cannot contain qualifying values.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: low and high.
output: The sum of values within the range.

examples.why: The values 7, 10 and 15 are in range: 32.

hints: If a node is below the low bound, its left subtree is useless.
DFS: if value < low go right only; if value > high go left only; otherwise add it and visit both.
approach: Recursive DFS using the BST property to prune: skip the left subtree when the node is below low and the right subtree when it is above high; add values in range.
complexity: O(h + k) time where k is the number of visited nodes in range

title: Search-tree ancestor
statement: Insert the values into a BST. For two values that are stored in the tree, find their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node having both in its subtree (a node counts as its own descendant).
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: two stored values.
output: The value of the lowest common ancestor.

examples.why: 5 is left of 10 and 15 is right of 10, so they split at 10.
They are on opposite sides of the root 20.

hints: Compare both values with the current node.
If both are smaller go left, if both are larger go right, otherwise the current node is the answer.
approach: Walk down from the root. While both values lie on the same side of the current node, move to that child. The first node where they split (or equal one of them) is the answer.

title: Floor and ceiling
statement: For a query number x, the floor in a BST is the largest stored value that is at most x and the ceiling is the smallest stored value that is at least x. Insert the values, then print the floor and the ceiling of x, using the word none where no such value exists.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: the query x.
output: Floor and ceiling separated by a space.

examples.why: The largest value ≤ 27 is 25 and the smallest ≥ 27 is 30.
Nothing is ≤ 1, and the smallest value ≥ 1 is 5: none 5.

hints: Each comparison narrows your candidate.
Walk from the root: if node ≤ x, it is a floor candidate and go right; otherwise go left. Do the mirror for ceiling.
approach: Descend from the root once for each of floor and ceiling. For the floor, record the node when value ≤ x and move right, else move left. For the ceiling record when value ≥ x and move left, else right.

title: Insertion height
statement: Build a BST by inserting the given distinct values in order and report the tree's height, counting the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. The order of insertion changes the shape, so it matters.
input: One line of distinct integers inserted in order.
output: The height as a number of nodes.

examples.why: 5-3-1-2 is the longest path with 4 nodes.
A perfectly balanced tree of 7 nodes has height 3.

hints: Build the tree first, then measure.
height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)).
approach: Insert each value with the standard BST rule, then compute the height recursively (or track depth during insertion and keep the maximum).
complexity: O(n*h) time to build, O(h) space

title: Next in order
statement: After inserting values into a BST, find the in-order successor of a stored value: the smallest stored value that is strictly greater than it. Print none if it is the largest.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: a stored value.
output: The successor's value, or none.

examples.why: 7 has no right subtree, so the successor is the ancestor 10.

hints: Two cases: the node has a right child, or it does not.
With a right child take its leftmost node; otherwise the answer is the last ancestor where you turned left.
approach: Walk down from the root toward the value. Whenever you go left from a node, remember that node as a candidate successor. If the target has a right subtree, the successor is the leftmost node in it.

title: k-th biggest score
statement: Given a list of scores, find the k-th largest one, counting duplicates separately (so in 5 5 5 the 2nd largest is 5). Try to do better than sorting the whole list when k is small.
input: Line 1: the scores. Line 2: k.
output: The k-th largest score.

examples.why: Descending order is 9 8 7 4 2 1, so the 3rd is 7.
Duplicates count: the 2nd largest is still 5.

hints: You only need to remember the k largest scores seen so far.
Keep a min-heap of size k; if it grows past k, pop the smallest. The root is the answer.
approach: Maintain a min-heap holding the k largest values. Push each score and pop when the heap exceeds k elements. After the scan the heap's top is the k-th largest.
complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space

title: Boulder smash
statement: Each round, take the two heaviest boulders and smash them together. If their weights are equal both vanish; otherwise the lighter vanishes and the heavier is left with the weight difference. Continue until at most one boulder remains and print its weight (0 if none).
input: One line of positive integers, the boulder weights.
output: The weight of the last boulder, or 0.

examples.why: 7 and 4 leave 3; then 3,3,3: two 3s vanish, one 3 remains.

hints: You repeatedly need the largest elements.
Use a max-heap (negate values in a min-heap): pop two, push back the difference if non-zero.
approach: Put all weights in a max-heap. While at least two remain, pop the two largest and push back their difference if it is non-zero. The heap's last element, if any, is the answer.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Most requested items
statement: A shop logs the ID of every item that was requested. Find the k most frequently requested IDs, most frequent first; if two IDs are requested equally often, the smaller ID comes first.
input: Line 1: the logged IDs. Line 2: k.
output: k IDs separated by spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct IDs ≤ n ≤ 10^5

examples.why: ID 1 appears 3 times and ID 2 twice.
4 and 5 tie with two requests, and the smaller ID 4 wins.

hints: Count first, then select.
Put (-count, id) in a heap of the distinct IDs, or keep a size-k heap keyed by count and ID.
approach: Count frequencies with a hash map, then use a heap (or a sort) keyed by (-count, id) to pull out the k best IDs.
complexity: O(n + d log k) time, O(d) space (d = distinct IDs)

title: Join the ropes
statement: You have ropes of various lengths and can tie two together at a cost equal to the sum of their lengths. Tie all ropes into a single rope while paying as little in total as possible, and print that minimum cost.
input: One line of positive integers, the rope lengths.
output: The minimum total cost.
hints: Long ropes should be involved in as few joins as possible.
Always join the two shortest ropes using a min-heap.
approach: Use a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the two shortest ropes, add their sum to the cost, and push the sum back, until one rope remains. This is the Huffman-style greedy.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Nearest to the origin
statement: Delivery drones are located at integer points on a plane. Find the k drones closest to the origin (0,0) by straight-line distance. Order them by distance, breaking ties by smaller x and then smaller y.
input: Line 1: k. Remaining lines: one point 'x y' per line.
output: k points written x,y separated by spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10^5; coordinates up to 10^4 in absolute value

examples.why: Squared distances are 10, 8, 89, 1, so the two nearest are (0,1) and (-2,2).
All are at squared distance 25; tie-break by x gives (-3,-4) then (3,4).

hints: You do not need the real distance, only a comparable value.
Compare squared distances; keep a max-heap of size k or sort.
approach: Compute squared distance for each point. Use a size-k max-heap (or sort) keyed by (distance, x, y) and output the k smallest in order.
complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space

title: Smooth numbers
statement: A number is smooth if its only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5 (the number 1 counts as smooth). Starting with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, ..., find the n-th smooth number in increasing order.
input: One line with the integer n.
output: The n-th smooth number.

examples.why: The sequence begins 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 9 10 12, so the 10th is 12.

hints: Every smooth number comes from a smaller smooth number times 2, 3 or 5.
Pop the smallest from a min-heap, push its multiples by 2, 3, 5 (avoid duplicates with a set).
approach: Start the heap with 1 and a visited set. Pop the smallest n-1 times, pushing x*2, x*3, x*5 when not seen. The next pop is the n-th number.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Valid min-heap
statement: A binary heap can be stored in an array where the children of index i sit at indices 2i+1 and 2i+2. Given an array, decide whether it is a valid min-heap: every parent must be less than or equal to each of its children.
input: One line of integers.
output: true or false.

examples.why: Each parent is no larger than its children.
Index 3 holds 2, which is smaller than its parent at index 1 (value 3).

hints: You only need to compare each node to its parent, or each parent to its children.
For i from 1 to n-1, check a[(i-1)//2] <= a[i].
approach: Loop over all indices i ≥ 1 and verify the parent at (i-1)//2 is not larger than a[i]. Any violation means the array is not a min-heap.

title: Build a heap by insertion
statement: Build a min-heap stored in an array by inserting numbers one at a time: append the new value at the end, then swap it with its parent while it is smaller than the parent (children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2). Print the array after all insertions.
input: One line of integers in insertion order.
output: The final heap array.

examples.why: After 5,3 the array is [3,5]; 8 stays; 1 swaps with 5 then with 3: 1 3 8 5.
Already in heap order, so nothing moves: 1 2 3 4.

hints: The parent of index i is (i-1)//2.
After appending, loop: while i > 0 and the parent is larger, swap and move up.
approach: For each value, append it to the array and sift it up by swapping with its parent while the parent is larger. The array after all insertions is the answer.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Stack with a minimum
statement: Design a stack that supports push x, pop, top and min in constant time, where min reports the smallest value currently stored. Simulate the commands; print one number for each top and min command.
input: One line of commands separated by semicolons. pop, top and min are only issued on a non-empty stack.
output: The results of top and min commands in order.

examples.why: Min is 3, still 3 with 7 on top, then after popping 7 and 3 the stack is just 5: 3 3 5 5.
Min -3; after popping -3 the top is 0 and the min is -2: -3 0 -2.

hints: What must you remember about the minimum when something is popped?
Store alongside each element the minimum of the stack up to that element (or use a second stack).
approach: Keep a second stack (or pair values) where each entry holds the minimum of all elements at or below it. push updates it with min(x, previous min); pop removes from both; min reads the top.

title: Five-second hit counter
statement: Design a counter that records hits with integer second timestamps and answers how many hits occurred in the last 5 seconds, i.e. with timestamps in [t-4, t], when asked at time t. Timestamps in the commands never decrease. Simulate hit t and count t commands, and print the answer of each count.
input: One line of commands separated by semicolons.
output: The results of count commands, space-separated.

examples.why: At 4 the window [0,4] holds 3 hits; at 8 the window [4,8] holds only the hit at 8; at 9 the window [5,9] holds it too: 3 1 1.
Window [1,5] holds three hits; window [2,6] holds none: 3 0.

hints: Old hits never matter again.
Keep a queue of timestamps; before counting, pop timestamps older than t-4.
approach: Store hit timestamps in a deque. On count t, drop timestamps below t-4 from the front and return the deque length. Each timestamp is added and removed once.
complexity: Amortised O(1) per operation, O(hits in window) space
edgeCases: Several hits in the same second

title: Browser trail
statement: Design a browser history that starts on a homepage. visit u opens a page and discards all forward history, back k moves back up to k pages (stopping at the oldest), and forward k moves forward up to k pages (stopping at the newest). After each back or forward command print the current page.
input: Line 1: the homepage name. Line 2: commands separated by semicolons.
output: The current page after each back/forward command, space-separated.

examples.why: Back from b gives a, back 5 stops at home, forward 1 gives a, visiting c clears forward history, so forward 2 stays on c: a home a c.
Back at the oldest page stays on start; after visit x forward does nothing; back returns to start: start x start.

hints: Treat history as an array with a cursor.
On visit truncate everything after the cursor, append, and move the cursor; clamp back/forward to valid bounds.
approach: Keep a list of pages and a current index. visit slices the list at index+1 and appends; back and forward adjust the index within [0, len-1] and report the page.
complexity: O(1) per back/forward, O(n) per visit with slicing; O(n) space

title: Ring buffer queue
statement: Design a queue with a fixed capacity, implemented on a circular array. enq x returns true and appends if there is room, otherwise false; deq removes and returns the front value or -1 if empty; front returns the front value or -1; isfull returns true or false. Print the result of every command.
input: Line 1: capacity. Line 2: commands separated by semicolons.
output: One result per command, space-separated.
