examples.why: The third enq fails; after deq 1 the queue is 2,3, front 2, and it is full: true true false 1 true 2 true.
deq on empty gives -1, then 4 fits, queue is full, deq returns 4, then empty again: -1 true true 4 -1.

hints: Use a head index and a size counter.
The tail slot is (head + size) % capacity; deq advances head modulo capacity.
approach: Allocate an array of the given capacity with head=0 and size=0. enq writes at (head+size)%cap when size<cap. deq reads at head and moves head forward modulo cap, decrementing size.

title: Moving average meter
statement: Design a meter with window size k that receives numbers one at a time and, after each, reports the average of the last k numbers received (or of all numbers if fewer than k have arrived). Print each average with exactly two decimals.
input: Line 1: k. Line 2: the values in arrival order.
output: One average per value, each with two decimal places.
hints: Recomputing the sum of the window each time is O(k).
Keep a running sum and a queue; subtract the value that leaves the window.
approach: Maintain a deque of the last k values and a running sum. Append each value, add it to the sum, and if the deque exceeds k remove the oldest value from both. The average is sum divided by deque length.

title: Pair-sum stream
statement: Design a structure that collects numbers with add x and answers find v: is there a pair of previously added numbers (two separate additions, equal values allowed if added twice) whose sum is v? Simulate the commands and print true or false for every find.
input: One line of commands separated by semicolons.
output: The results of find commands, space-separated.
constraints: up to 10^4 commands; values up to 10^6 in absolute value

examples.why: 1+3=4 works; no pair makes 7; after a second 3, 3+3=6 works; no pair makes 2: true false true false.
One 2 cannot pair with itself; two 2s can: false true.

hints: A frequency map lets add run in O(1).
For find, loop over distinct stored values x and look up v-x; if v-x == x you need a count of at least 2.
approach: Store counts in a hash map. add increments a count. find iterates the distinct values x, checks whether v-x exists with count >= 2 when it equals x, or at least 1 otherwise.
complexity: O(1) add, O(d) find (d distinct values)

title: Stack with a bonus
statement: Design a stack with a maximum size. push x does nothing when the stack is full, pop returns the top or -1 if empty, and inc k v adds v to each of the bottom k elements (or all of them if fewer than k exist). Print the result of every pop.
input: Line 1: maximum size. Line 2: commands separated by semicolons.
output: The results of pop commands, space-separated.

examples.why: The stack [1,2,3] gets +100 on all three; pops return 2, 103, 102, 101, -1 (push 4 was ignored): 2 103 102 101 -1.
The only element rises from 5 to 8: 8.

hints: A direct loop for inc is fine at these limits; can you make it O(1)?
Lazy increments: store a pending add per index and push it down to the element below when popping.
approach: Use an array stack with a parallel array of lazy increments. inc adds v to the lazy slot at index min(k,size)-1. On pop, return value plus its lazy amount and add the lazy amount to the slot below.
complexity: O(1) per operation with lazy increments, O(max size) space
edgeCases: inc with k larger than size

title: Phone number pool
statement: A company owns phone numbers 0..n-1. get hands out the smallest free number (or -1 if none are left), check x says whether x is currently free, and release x makes a handed-out number free again (releasing a free number does nothing). Print the result of every get and check.
input: Line 1: n. Line 2: commands separated by semicolons.
output: Results of get and check commands, space-separated.

examples.why: Hand out 0 and 1; 1 is taken; after releasing 0, get returns 0, then 2, then -1: 0 1 false 0 2 -1.
Free, take it, taken, released, free again: true 0 false true.

hints: You need the smallest free number quickly.
Keep a min-heap of free numbers and a set of used ones.
approach: Store free numbers in a min-heap and handed-out numbers in a set. get pops the heap and records the number; release pushes it back if it was in use; check tests set membership.
complexity: O(log n) per get/release, O(1) check
edgeCases: Release then get returns the same number

title: Undo-redo notepad
statement: Design a text pad. type w appends the word w (no spaces), undo reverts the most recent typing that has not been undone, redo reapplies the most recently undone typing, and typing anything new clears the redo history. show prints the current text, or EMPTY if it is empty. Undo and redo do nothing when there is nothing to undo or redo.
input: One line of commands separated by semicolons.
output: The text at each show command, space-separated.

examples.why: After undo only ab; redo restores abcd; two undos empty the pad: ab abcd EMPTY.
Typing y cleared the redo history, so the first redo does nothing and show gives y; undo empties the pad; the later redo brings y back: y EMPTY y.

hints: Two stacks model history: one for done actions, one for undone ones.
Typing pushes on the undo stack and clears the redo stack; undo moves an item between stacks.
approach: Keep an undo stack and a redo stack of typed words and a text buffer. type appends, pushes on undo and clears redo; undo pops and removes that word from the end; redo pops from redo and re-appends. show prints the buffer.
complexity: O(len) per command in the worst case

title: Flip rows and columns
statement: Transpose a rectangular matrix: the element in row i, column j of the input moves to row j, column i of the output. A matrix with r rows and c columns becomes one with c rows and r columns.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: The transposed matrix, one row per line.

examples.why: The two rows become two columns of a 3x2 matrix.
A square matrix reflects across its main diagonal.

hints: The output shape is the input shape swapped.
Create an empty c x r matrix and set out[j][i] = in[i][j].
approach: Allocate a c-by-r result and copy each element a[i][j] into result[j][i]. In-place transposition is only possible for square matrices.

title: Quarter turn
statement: Rotate a rectangular matrix 90 degrees clockwise and print the result. The top row of the input becomes the rightmost column of the output.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: The rotated matrix, one row per line.

examples.why: The left column read bottom-up becomes the top row: 3 1 / 4 2.

hints: Rotating clockwise equals transposing and then reversing each row.
Or use out[j][r-1-i] = in[i][j].
approach: Transpose the matrix and reverse every row of the transpose; equivalently map a[i][j] to result[j][r-1-i].

title: Spiral walk
statement: Start at the top-left cell of a matrix and walk clockwise around it in a spiral - right along the top, down the right side, left along the bottom, up the left side - then continue inwards. Print the values in the order you visit them.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: All values in spiral order on one line.

examples.why: A single row is read left to right.

hints: Track four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
Walk one side at a time, shrinking the matching boundary after each side, and stop when boundaries cross.
approach: Maintain top, bottom, left and right indices. Traverse the top row, right column, bottom row (if rows remain) and left column (if columns remain), moving each boundary inwards after its pass.
complexity: O(r*c) time, O(1) extra space besides output

title: Diagonal total
statement: For a square matrix, add up the numbers on both diagonals. The centre cell of an odd-sized matrix lies on both, so count it only once.
input: A square matrix, each line a row.
output: The diagonal sum.

examples.why: Diagonals give 1+5+9 and 3+7 with the centre counted once: 25.

hints: Indices on the main diagonal satisfy i == j; on the anti-diagonal i + j == n-1.
Sum a[i][i] + a[i][n-1-i] for each row, then subtract the centre if n is odd.
approach: Loop over rows adding the main and anti-diagonal entries. If n is odd the middle cell was added twice, so subtract it once.

title: Cross out zeros
statement: Whenever a matrix cell holds 0, every cell in its row and its column must become 0. Zeros created by this rule must not trigger further changes - decide using the original matrix only. Print the resulting matrix.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: The updated matrix, one row per line.

examples.why: The zero at the centre clears its row and column.
The zero in the corner clears the first row and first column.

hints: Record first, modify later.
Collect the set of rows and columns containing a zero, then zero them in a second pass.
approach: First pass: note every row and column index that contains a zero. Second pass: set a cell to 0 if its row or column is marked. (Marker rows and columns inside the matrix give O(1) extra space.)

title: Matrix product
statement: Multiply an r x k matrix A by a k x c matrix B. Entry (i, j) of the product is the sum over t of A[i][t] * B[t][j]. The two matrices are separated by a line containing three dashes.
input: Matrix A, a line '---', then matrix B.
output: The r x c product, one row per line.
constraints: 1 ≤ r, k, c ≤ 100; products fit in 64-bit

examples.why: A 1x3 times a 3x1 gives the single number 6.

hints: Each output cell is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B.
Use three nested loops over i, j, t.
approach: For every cell (i, j) of the result, sum A[i][t]*B[t][j] over t. Three nested loops cover everything.

title: Constant diagonals
statement: A matrix is called diagonal-constant if every diagonal running from top-left to bottom-right holds one repeated value. Decide whether the given matrix has this property.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: true or false.

examples.why: Each top-left to bottom-right diagonal is constant.

hints: Two cells share a diagonal if one is the other's up-left neighbour.
Check that a[i][j] == a[i-1][j-1] for all i, j ≥ 1.
approach: Compare each cell with its up-left neighbour; if any pair differs the property fails. All other cells are covered by the chain of neighbours.
edgeCases: One bad cell at the bottom right

title: Saddle values
statement: A saddle value is a number that is the smallest in its row and, at the same time, the largest in its column. All numbers in the matrix are distinct. Print every saddle value in increasing order, or none if there are none.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: Saddle values separated by spaces, or none.

examples.why: Only 6 is the minimum of its row and the maximum of its column.
Row minima 1 and 2 are not column maxima: none.

hints: Find each row's minimum first.
Precompute column maxima; compare each row minimum against the maximum of its column.
approach: Compute the minimum of every row and the maximum of every column. A row minimum whose value equals the maximum of its column is a saddle value.

title: Count the friend clusters
statement: A school has n students numbered 1..n. Some pairs are direct friends, and friendship spreads: friends of friends, and so on, all belong to one cluster. Count how many clusters exist (a student with no friends is a cluster by themselves).
input: First line n and m, followed by m lines each with two student numbers u v.
output: One integer: the number of clusters.

examples.why: Nobody is friends, so each student is alone.

hints: Think of students as nodes and friendships as undirected edges.
Walk from each unvisited node with BFS or DFS and count how many walks you start.
approach: Build adjacency lists and run an iterative DFS/BFS from each unvisited node, counting starts. A union-find structure works equally well.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space

title: Fewest hops between stations
statement: A subway has n stations connected by two-way tunnels. Every tunnel takes one hop regardless of length. Find the smallest number of hops needed to get from station a to station b, or report that you cannot get there.
input: First line n m a b, followed by m lines each with a tunnel u v.
output: The minimum number of hops, or -1 if b is unreachable.
hints: Every edge costs the same, so which traversal order finds shortest routes first?
Use BFS from a and record distances; unvisited means unreachable.
approach: Run BFS from a, storing the distance when each node is first discovered. The distance of b is the answer, or -1 if it was never reached.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
edgeCases: Direct tunnel between a and b

title: Rooms and their keys
statement: A mansion has n rooms numbered 0..n-1, and only room 0 is unlocked at the start. Each room contains some keys, and each key opens exactly one room (keys can be reused and never break). Decide whether you can eventually enter every room.
input: First line n; then n lines, line i starting with a count c followed by c room numbers, the keys found in room i.
output: YES if every room can be entered, otherwise NO.

examples.why: Room 0 gives keys to 1 and 2, room 1 gives a key to 3.
Nobody holds a key to room 2, so it stays locked.

hints: Rooms are nodes, and a key in room i for room j is a directed edge i -> j.
Run a DFS/BFS from room 0 and compare the visited count with n.
approach: Treat keys as directed edges and traverse from room 0 with a stack, marking rooms visited. If all n rooms get visited the answer is YES.
edgeCases: Keys pointing back to already visited rooms
Room with no keys that blocks progress

title: The busiest airport
statement: An airline flies direct routes between n airports, each route usable in both directions and listed once. The busiest airport is the one with the most routes touching it. Print that airport and its route count; if several tie, choose the smallest number.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with two airports u v.
output: Two integers: the busiest airport and its degree.

examples.why: Airports 1 and 2 tie with one route, pick 1.

hints: You do not need adjacency lists, only counts.
Add one to both endpoints per edge, then scan for the maximum.
approach: Keep a degree array, incrementing both endpoints per edge. Scan from index 1 upward keeping the first index with the strictly largest degree.

title: Find the quiet mayor
statement: In a village of n people, a line a b means person a trusts person b (one direction only). The mayor trusts nobody, yet everybody else trusts the mayor. Find the mayor, or report that there is none.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a b meaning a trusts b.
output: The mayor's number, or -1 if no one qualifies.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5; 0 ≤ m ≤ 3·10^5; no duplicate lines, a ≠ b

examples.why: Person 3 trusts nobody and is trusted by both others.
Everyone trusts someone, so there is no mayor.

hints: Count how many people each person trusts and how many trust them.
The mayor has out-degree 0 and in-degree n-1.
approach: Compute in-degree and out-degree arrays in one pass over the edges, then return the node with out 0 and in n-1. At most one node can satisfy this.
edgeCases: n = 1 and m = 0 (the lone person is mayor)
Everyone trusts the mayor but the mayor trusts someone

title: Who is within reach
statement: A rumor starts at person a and each day passes along every two-way acquaintance link from people who already know it. After exactly k days, how many people other than a know the rumor? Everyone connected by a path of at most k links hears it.
input: First line n m a k, followed by m lines each with a link u v.
output: One integer: the count of people (excluding a) within k links of a.

examples.why: Within two links of 1 are 2 and 3.
All three neighbors are one link away.

hints: BFS gives the minimum number of links to each person.
Count nodes whose distance is between 1 and k.
approach: Run BFS from a to get distances, then count nodes other than a whose distance is at most k. Unreached nodes are never counted.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space

title: Is this network a tree
statement: A network of n servers is joined by m two-way cables. It is called tree-shaped if every server can reach every other and removing any cable would break that. Decide whether the network is tree-shaped.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a cable u v.
output: YES if the network is tree-shaped, otherwise NO.

examples.why: A simple chain: connected with n-1 cables.
Three cables but server 4 is cut off and there is a loop.

hints: A tree on n nodes always has exactly n-1 edges.
Having n-1 edges is not enough; also check that everything is connected.
approach: Reject immediately unless m = n-1. Then check connectivity with BFS/DFS or union-find; connected plus n-1 edges implies no cycles.

title: Reachable from both
statement: A city has n bus stops and m one-way bus lines. Two friends start at stops a and b. Count how many stops (including their own start stops, if applicable) can be reached by both friends using any number of bus lines.
input: First line n m a b, followed by m lines each with a one-way line u v.
output: One integer: the number of stops reachable from both a and b.

examples.why: Each only reaches its own start, no overlap.

hints: Do one traversal per friend and keep each visited set.
Intersect the two sets and count.
approach: Run a directed DFS from a and another from b, producing two visited arrays. The answer is the number of nodes marked in both.
edgeCases: a and b can reach each other

title: Fence around the garden
statement: A map shows a field as R rows and C columns, where # is a planted plot and . is bare soil. A fence is needed along every plot side that does not touch another plot (map edges count as open). Compute the total fence length, with each plot side having length 1.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters each.
output: One integer: the total fence length.

examples.why: A plus shape has 12 exposed sides.
A lone plot has four sides.

hints: Look at each plot cell separately.
For each of its four neighbors, add 1 if it is outside the map or not a plot.
approach: Scan every # cell and count the neighbors (up, down, left, right) that are out of bounds or not #. The sum is the answer; no traversal is needed.

title: The biggest forest patch
statement: A satellite image is a grid where # marks forest and . marks open ground. Forest cells touching up, down, left or right belong to the same patch. Report the number of cells in the largest patch, or 0 if there is no forest.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters each.
output: One integer: the size of the largest patch.

examples.why: The left patch has 3 cells, the right one has 3; largest is 3.

hints: Flood from an unvisited # cell and count what you reach.
Use an explicit stack or queue to avoid deep recursion on big grids.
approach: For each unvisited # cell run a DFS/BFS over 4-neighbors counting cells, and track the maximum count seen.
edgeCases: Diagonal-only contact does not join patches

title: Steps through the maze
statement: A maze is drawn on a grid: S is the start, E is the exit, . is open floor and # is wall. Each move goes one cell up, down, left or right onto a non-wall cell. Find the fewest moves needed to reach E from S, or -1 if it cannot be done.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters with exactly one S and one E.
output: The minimum number of moves, or -1.

examples.why: Down, down, right, right, right is 5 moves.
The wall column blocks every route.

hints: All moves cost the same, so use breadth-first search.
Store distance per cell when you first enqueue it.
approach: BFS from S over open cells, recording distance on first visit. Return the distance when E is dequeued, or -1 if the queue empties.

title: Paint bucket tool
statement: A tiny image is a grid of letters, each letter being a color. A paint bucket click at a given cell replaces that cell's color, and every cell connected to it through up/down/left/right neighbors of the same original color, with a new color. Print the image after the click.
input: First line R C, then R image rows, then a line r c ch with a 1-indexed cell and the new letter.
output: The R rows of the image after painting.

examples.why: The connected a-region {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)} becomes z; the a at (3,3) is separate.
New color equals old color, nothing changes.

hints: Remember the original color before overwriting anything.
If the new color equals the old one, stop early to avoid an endless loop.
approach: Read the target cell's color, then DFS/BFS over 4-neighbors with that same color, overwriting each as it is visited. Overwriting doubles as the visited mark.
edgeCases: Click on a single isolated cell

title: Islands that touch at corners
statement: On a map, # is land and . is water. Two land cells belong to the same island if they share a side or a corner (so eight directions). Count the islands.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: One integer: the number of islands.

examples.why: The three cells touch diagonally, so one island.
Four corner cells are not adjacent in any direction.

hints: This is ordinary component counting with a bigger neighbor list.
Use the 8 offsets (dx,dy) with dx,dy in {-1,0,1} except (0,0).
approach: Count connected components of # cells using DFS/BFS with eight neighbor offsets, marking cells visited as you go.

title: Count the lonely stars
statement: A night-sky chart is a grid where * is a star and . is empty sky. A star is lonely if none of the four cells directly above, below, left or right of it also holds a star. Count the lonely stars.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: One integer: the number of lonely stars.

examples.why: (1,1), (3,1) and (3,4) are lonely; the pair at the top right is not.
The ends and middle all have a star neighbor.

hints: You only need to inspect the four direct neighbors.
Guard against stepping outside the grid.
approach: Visit each * and check its four neighbors with bounds checks. Count the stars that have none.
edgeCases: Single cell grid with a star

title: How much can the explorer see
statement: A robot starts on the cell marked S of a grid where . is floor and # is wall. It moves one cell at a time up, down, left or right and cannot enter walls. Count how many distinct cells it can ever stand on, including its starting cell.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters with exactly one S.
output: One integer: the number of reachable cells.

examples.why: Only S and its two neighbors are reachable.

hints: Keep a visited set so each cell is counted once.
DFS or BFS both work.
approach: Flood fill from S over non-wall cells and return the number of visited cells.

title: Fill in the mine numbers
statement: A minefield grid marks mines with * and safe cells with . . Replace every safe cell with the number of mines among its up to eight surrounding cells, keeping mines as *. Print the resulting board.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: R lines of the completed board.

examples.why: Middle top cell touches both mines, the others touch one.
Both safe cells touch the one mine.

hints: Loop over all cells and look in 8 directions.
A mine cell is never replaced.
approach: For each non-mine cell count mine cells among the eight neighbors with bounds checks, then write the digit. A single pass over the grid suffices.
complexity: O(R·C) time, O(R·C) space for output

title: Does the water seep through
statement: Water is poured over the top of a rock slab drawn as a grid, where . is a pore and # is solid rock. Water flows from any pore in the top row to adjacent pores (up, down, left, right). Decide whether it can reach any pore in the bottom row.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: YES if water reaches the bottom row, otherwise NO.

examples.why: Down the left column then along the bottom.
The pores at the top and bottom only touch diagonally.

hints: Start the traversal from every pore of the top row at once.
Return as soon as you pop a cell in the last row.
approach: Multi-source DFS/BFS seeded with all top-row pores over 4-neighbors. If any visited cell is in row R-1, the answer is YES.

title: How many work crews
statement: A site has n workers. Each statement a b says workers a and b are on the same crew, and crew membership is transitive. After reading all statements, how many distinct crews are there? A worker never mentioned forms a crew alone.
input: First line n k, then k lines each with a statement a b.
output: One integer: the number of crews.

examples.why: Everyone is in one crew; the last statement adds nothing.

hints: Start with n separate groups and merge on every statement.
A union-find structure tracks the group count cheaply.
approach: Initialize a disjoint-set forest with n singleton sets and a counter n. Each successful union of two different roots decrements the counter.
complexity: O((n + k) α(n)) time, O(n) space
edgeCases: A statement linking a worker to themselves

title: Are they on the same crew
statement: Workers 1..n start on separate crews. You receive a mixed list of operations: U a b merges the crews of a and b, and Q a b asks whether a and b are currently on the same crew. Answer every query at the moment it is asked.
input: First line n q, then q lines each starting with U or Q followed by two worker numbers.
output: One line YES or NO for each Q, in order.

examples.why: Queries: no, yes, then 1 and 3 joined through 2.
A worker is always with themselves; 1 and 2 are never merged.

hints: Compare the representatives of both workers.
Use path compression to keep find fast.
approach: Use union-find: U performs union, Q compares find(a) and find(b). Path compression plus union by size makes each operation near constant time.

title: Size of the biggest crew
statement: People at a festival form groups through introductions: an introduction a b puts a and b in the same group, and groups merge transitively. After all introductions, how many people are in the largest group?
input: First line n m, then m lines each with an introduction a b.
output: One integer: the size of the largest group.
hints: Keep a size counter for each set root.
When merging, add the size of the absorbed set.
approach: Maintain size[root] in a union-find. After all unions, take the maximum size over roots.
complexity: O((n + m) α(n)) time, O(n) space

title: The cable that closes a loop
statement: Cables are laid one at a time between n posts. A cable is redundant if its two posts were already linked, directly or indirectly, by earlier cables. Print the first redundant cable as its two posts, or NONE if every cable added a new connection.
input: First line n m, then m lines each with a cable a b in the order laid.
output: The first redundant cable as 'a b', or NONE.

examples.why: The fourth cable joins posts already connected.

hints: Process in the given order; stop at the first problem.
Union returns false when both ends already share a root.
approach: Run union-find over cables in order. The first union that finds equal roots is the answer; otherwise print NONE.
edgeCases: Duplicate cable as the first redundant one

title: Groups after every merge
statement: n islands start disconnected. Bridges are built one by one, and a bridge a b joins the land masses of a and b. After each bridge, report how many separate land masses remain.
input: First line n m, then m lines each with a bridge a b in construction order.
output: m space-separated integers: the land-mass count after each bridge.

examples.why: Repeated bridges do not reduce the count again.

hints: The count only changes when a union actually merges two sets.
Record the counter after each edge.
approach: Union-find with a component counter; append the counter to the result after processing each bridge.
complexity: O(m α(n)) time, O(n + m) space

title: Moving spare cables
statement: A lab has n computers and m existing cables, each joining two computers. You may unplug any cable and replug it between any two computers. Find the minimum number of replugs needed to make all computers connected, or -1 if there are too few cables for that to be possible.
input: First line n m, then m lines each with a cable a b.
output: The minimum number of moves, or -1.

examples.why: Components {1,2},{3,4}; the duplicate cable can be moved once.
Four cables are required for five computers but only two exist.

hints: To connect c components you need c-1 new links.
If m < n-1 it can never be connected.
approach: Count components with union-find. If m < n-1 return -1; otherwise return components - 1, since surplus cables always exist to be moved.
complexity: O((n + m) α(n)) time, O(n) space

title: Circles from a matrix
statement: n people are described by an n by n table where entry (i,j) is 1 if person i knows person j directly. Knowing is symmetric and a circle contains everyone linked through chains of acquaintances. Count the circles.
input: First line n, then n lines of n space-separated 0/1 values.
output: One integer: the number of circles.

examples.why: Persons 1 and 2 form a circle; 3 is alone.
Only the diagonal is set, so three circles.

hints: Every 1 off the diagonal is an edge.
Union i and j for each such entry.
approach: Scan the matrix, union (i,j) whenever the entry is 1, and report the number of remaining sets.

title: Label each cluster by its smallest member
statement: Towns 1..n are linked by m two-way roads. Give each town the label of its region: the smallest town number in the set of towns reachable from it. Print the label of every town.
input: First line n m, then m lines each with a road a b.
output: n space-separated labels, one per town in order.

examples.why: Each town is its own region.

hints: Union-find roots are arbitrary; keep your own minimum per root.
Or always union so the smaller index becomes the root.
approach: Build a union-find, then compute the smallest index for each root in one pass and map each node to its root's minimum.
complexity: O((n + m) α(n)) time, O(n) space

title: Fewest notes and coins
statement: A cash register holds unlimited notes and coins worth 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100. For a given payout amount, find the smallest number of pieces that add up to exactly that amount.
input: One integer a.
output: One integer: the minimum number of pieces.
hints: Try the largest piece first.
For this particular set of values, taking the largest piece that fits is always optimal.
approach: Greedily take as many of the largest denomination as fit, then move to the next. This set is canonical, so greedy is optimal.

title: Attend the most talks
statement: At a conference there are n talks, each with a start and end time. You can attend a talk only entirely, and you may begin a talk at the exact moment another one ends. Find the largest number of talks you can attend.
input: First line n, then n lines each with start end.
output: One integer: the maximum number of talks.

examples.why: Skip the long talk and take the two short ones.

hints: Sort by something other than start time.
Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the future.
approach: Sort talks by end time and greedily accept each talk whose start is at least the end of the last accepted one.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Hand out the cookies
statement: Children each demand a minimum cookie size, and you have cookies of various sizes. Each child gets at most one cookie and each cookie goes to at most one child. A child is content if the cookie is at least as large as their demand. Maximize the number of content children.
input: First line n m; second line n demands; third line m cookie sizes.
output: One integer: the maximum number of content children.

examples.why: Both cookies have size 1, so only one child can be made content.
Cookie 1 for demand 1, cookie 2 for demand 2.

hints: Sort both lists.
Give each cookie to the least demanding unsatisfied child it can satisfy.
approach: Sort demands and sizes, walk through cookies in increasing size with a pointer into demands, advancing the pointer when a cookie satisfies the current child.
complexity: O(n log n + m log m) time, O(1) extra space

title: Can you reach the last stone
statement: Stones are laid in a row, and standing on stone i lets you jump forward by any distance from 0 to a[i]. Starting on the first stone, decide whether you can reach the last one.
input: First line n; second line n non-negative integers a[i].
output: YES if the last stone is reachable, otherwise NO.

examples.why: Jump 1 to stone 2, then 3 steps to the end.
Every path gets stuck at the zero.

hints: Track the farthest index reachable so far.
If you reach an index beyond that farthest point, you are stuck.
approach: Scan left to right keeping far = max(far, i + a[i]). If i exceeds far at any step the answer is NO; otherwise YES.
edgeCases: Zero at the start with n > 1

title: Collect every price rise
statement: You know a stock's price for each of n days. You may buy and sell as often as you like, but hold at most one share and must sell before buying again. Compute the maximum total profit.
input: First line n; second line n daily prices.
output: One integer: the maximum profit.

examples.why: Buy at 1 sell at 5, buy at 3 sell at 6: 4 + 3 = 7.
Prices only fall, so no trades.

hints: Consider each pair of adjacent days.
A multi-day climb equals the sum of its daily rises.
approach: Sum every positive difference between consecutive days. This equals the best set of non-overlapping trades.

title: Flip signs for the biggest total
statement: You have n numbers and must perform exactly k operations. Each operation picks one number (the same one may be chosen again) and multiplies it by -1. Choose operations to maximize the sum of the numbers afterwards.
input: First line n k; second line n integers.
output: One integer: the maximum possible sum.

examples.why: Flip the smallest number three times, leaving -1+2+3 = 4.

hints: Flipping a negative number to positive always helps.
If flips remain after all negatives are gone, only parity matters.
approach: Sort ascending, flip the most negative numbers first while k lasts. If an odd number of flips remain, subtract twice the smallest absolute value.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Lifeboats for everyone
statement: People with known weights must cross a river in boats. Each boat carries at most two people and a total weight of at most L. Every person's weight is at most L. Find the minimum number of boats.
input: First line n L; second line n weights.
output: One integer: the minimum number of boats.

examples.why: No two can share, so three boats.

hints: Sort the weights.
Try to pair the heaviest remaining person with the lightest.
approach: Sort and use two pointers: the heaviest always boards; the lightest joins if the sum fits. Count boats until pointers cross.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Cut into balanced pieces
statement: A string made only of the letters L and R has an equal number of each. Cut it into the largest possible number of consecutive pieces so that every piece also has equally many L and R. Print that number of pieces.
input: One string of L and R with equal counts.
output: One integer: the maximum number of pieces.

examples.why: Cutting inside breaks the balance; one piece.

hints: Treat L as +1 and R as -1 and watch the running total.
Each time the total returns to 0, you can end a piece.
approach: Maintain a running balance; whenever it hits zero, finish a piece and increment the counter. Cutting at every zero maximizes pieces.

title: Digit total by recursion
statement: Write a function that returns the sum of the decimal digits of a non-negative integer n without using loops or string conversion; the function should call itself on a smaller number. Print the digit sum of the given n.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer: the sum of its digits.

examples.why: Zero has digit sum 0, the base case.

hints: What is the answer for n = 0? That is your base case.
The last digit is n % 10 and the rest is n // 10.
approach: sum(n) = 0 when n = 0, otherwise n % 10 + sum(n // 10). Depth is at most 19.
complexity: O(log n) time, O(log n) stack

title: Fast power with a remainder
statement: Compute a raised to the power b, taken modulo m, using recursion that halves the exponent each time (so that b up to 10^18 is fine). Print the remainder.
input: One line with three integers a b m.
output: One integer: a^b mod m.
hints: a^b = (a^(b/2))^2 when b is even; multiply by a once more when odd.
Reduce modulo m after every multiplication.
approach: pow(a,b): if b = 0 return 1 mod m; let h = pow(a, b//2); return h·h mod m, times a mod m when b is odd. Depth is about 60.
complexity: O(log b) time, O(log b) stack

title: Does the word mirror itself
statement: A word reads the same forwards and backwards if it is a palindrome. Decide recursively: a word is a palindrome if its first and last letters match and the part between them is also a palindrome. Report the result for a lowercase word.
input: One lowercase word.
output: YES if palindrome, otherwise NO.
hints: Define the check on the index range (i, j).
Stop with true when the range has 0 or 1 letters.
approach: check(i,j) = true if i ≥ j, else w[i] == w[j] and check(i+1, j-1).

title: Rabbit pair growth
statement: A farmer's rabbit population follows R(0) = 0, R(1) = 1 and R(k) = R(k-1) + R(k-2) for k ≥ 2. Compute R(n) with recursion, making sure you do not recompute the same value over and over.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer: R(n).
hints: The naive version makes an exponential number of calls.
Store computed values in a map or array (memoization).
approach: Recursive function with a memo table so each R(k) is computed once. Answers fit in 64-bit up to n = 90.

title: Tower of discs
statement: There are three pegs A, B, C and n discs of different sizes stacked on A with the smallest on top. Move all discs to peg C, moving one disc at a time and never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. Print one shortest sequence of moves, using the standard recursive scheme (move n-1 to the spare peg, move the largest, move n-1 on top).
input: One integer n.
output: One move per line as X->Y (source peg, destination peg).

examples.why: A single disc goes straight to C.

examples.out:
A->C
A->B
C->B
A->C
B->A
B->C
A->C
examples.why: Seven moves, built from the two-disc solution twice around the biggest disc.

hints: To move n discs from X to Z via Y, first solve it for n-1 from X to Y.
Then move the largest disc X->Z and solve n-1 from Y to Z.
approach: solve(n,X,Y,Z): if n = 0 return; solve(n-1,X,Z,Y); output X->Z; solve(n-1,Y,X,Z). This takes 2^n - 1 moves, the minimum.

title: List all bit strings
statement: Print every binary string of length n, one per line, in increasing order (as if reading them as binary numbers). Build them recursively one character at a time.
input: One integer n.
output: 2^n lines, each a binary string of length n.
hints: At each position you choose 0 or 1.
Try 0 before 1 to get increasing order.
approach: Recursive function building a prefix; when its length reaches n, output it; otherwise recurse with '0' appended then '1'.

title: Euclid and its calls
statement: Euclid's method is gcd(a, b) = a if b = 0, otherwise gcd(b, a mod b). Run it recursively on two integers and report both the gcd and the total number of calls to the function made, counting the first call and the final one with b = 0.
input: One line with integers a and b.
output: Two integers: the gcd and the number of calls.

examples.why: Immediately hits the base case: gcd 7, 1 call.

hints: Count by incrementing a counter at the top of the function.
Note a < b swaps them on the first step.
approach: Implement gcd recursively with a counter incremented per call. The number of calls is O(log min(a,b)).

title: Hailstone length
statement: Start from n. If the current number is even, halve it; if odd, replace it by 3 times itself plus 1. Count the steps until the value becomes 1. Implement it as a recursive function.
input: One integer n.
output: The number of steps to reach 1.
hints: The base case is n = 1.
One step plus the answer for the next value.
approach: steps(1) = 0; steps(n) = 1 + steps(next(n)). The sequence is finite for the allowed inputs and fits in 64-bit integers.

title: Ruler tick heights
statement: A ruler of order n has 2^n - 1 tick marks. The middle tick has height n, and each half is a ruler of order n-1. List the heights of the ticks from left to right.
input: One integer n.
output: The tick heights separated by spaces.

examples.why: 1 2 1: a middle tick of height 2 flanked by order-1 rulers.
Order-2 ruler, then 3, then order-2 ruler again.

hints: The pattern is self-similar.
ruler(n) = ruler(n-1) + [n] + ruler(n-1), with ruler(0) empty.
approach: Build the list recursively as left half, middle value n, right half. Output length is 2^n - 1.

title: How deep do the brackets nest
statement: A string of balanced parentheses is given, such as (()(())). Its nesting depth is the largest number of parentheses open at the same time. Compute it by recursing into each parenthesized group. An empty string has depth 0.
input: One line with a balanced parentheses string (possibly empty).
output: One integer: the maximum nesting depth.

examples.why: The innermost pair sits three levels deep.
Pairs are side by side, depth 1.

hints: The depth of a group is 1 plus the deepest group inside it.
Sibling groups combine with max, not with a sum.
approach: Parse recursively: a group starts at '(', parses inner groups until the matching ')', and returns 1 + max child depth. The top level takes the max over siblings.

title: Every possible team
statement: Given n distinct integers, list every subset (including the empty one). Sort the numbers first; print each subset in increasing order, and list subsets in lexicographic order, so a shorter prefix comes before its extensions (for 1 2: empty, 1, 1 2, 2). Print the empty subset as a single dash.
input: First line n; second line n distinct integers.
output: One subset per line, numbers separated by spaces; '-' for the empty subset.
hints: Decide include/exclude, or pick the next element from a start index.
Record the current path at every node of the recursion, not just at the leaves.
approach: DFS with a start index: record the current subset, then for each later element append it, recurse and pop. Sorting up front gives lexicographic order.

title: Every lineup order
statement: n runners numbered 1 to n line up in every possible order. Print all orderings (permutations) in lexicographic order, one per line.
input: One integer n.
output: n! lines, each with the n numbers separated by spaces.
hints: Keep a boolean array of numbers already used.
Trying numbers in increasing order at each position gives lexicographic output.
approach: Recursive fill of positions 1..n: for each unused number, place it, recurse, then undo. Output when the arrangement is complete.

title: Choose a team of k
statement: From players numbered 1 to n, list every team of exactly k players. Each team is written in increasing order and teams are listed in lexicographic order.
input: One line with n and k.
output: One team per line, numbers separated by spaces.
hints: After choosing x, the next member must be larger than x.
Stop early when the team has k members.
approach: DFS choosing the next member from a start index; when the team size reaches k record it. Optionally prune when too few players remain.
edgeCases: Pruning when not enough players remain

title: Pick items to hit the weight
statement: You have n items with positive weights. Decide whether some subset of the items weighs exactly T in total. A target of 0 is always possible by taking nothing.
input: First line n T; second line n positive integers.
output: YES if a subset sums to T, otherwise NO.
hints: For each item either take it or skip it.
Stop when the remainder reaches 0 or goes negative.
approach: Recursive take/skip search with the remaining target. Returns true as soon as the remainder is exactly 0; prune when it goes negative.

title: All balanced bracket patterns
statement: Print every well-formed string made of n pairs of parentheses, in the order where '(' comes before ')'. A string is well-formed if every prefix has at least as many '(' as ')' and the totals match.
input: One integer n.
output: One string per line, in lexicographic order with '(' < ')'.
hints: Only add ')' when there is an unmatched '('.
Only add '(' while fewer than n have been used.
approach: Backtrack building the string with counts of opens and closes; branch '(' if opens < n and ')' if closes < opens. This generates only valid strings.

title: Old phone keypad words
statement: On an old phone keypad, 2=abc, 3=def, 4=ghi, 5=jkl, 6=mno, 7=pqrs, 8=tuv and 9=wxyz. For a string of digits 2-9, list every letter string that could have been typed, in alphabetical order, on a single line separated by spaces.
input: One string of digits from 2 to 9.
output: All combinations separated by spaces, in alphabetical order.

examples.out: ad ae af bd be bf cd ce cf

hints: Each digit gives a small set of choices.
Recurse on the next digit for each letter.
approach: DFS over digit positions, appending each letter of the current digit to the prefix. Emit at full length. Iterating letters in order yields alphabetical output.

title: Ways to pay with repeats
statement: You have n distinct coin values, each available in unlimited quantity. List every multiset of coins that adds up exactly to T. Write each combination in non-decreasing order of values, and list the combinations in lexicographic order. If there are none, print NONE.
input: First line n T; second line n distinct positive integers.
output: One combination per line, or NONE.

examples.why: 2+2+3 is the only way; using 6 would leave 1, which no coin makes.

hints: Allow choosing the same coin again by recursing with the same index.
Keep coins sorted so you can stop when a coin exceeds the remainder.
approach: DFS with a start index (not incremented after choosing a coin) and remaining amount; record when it hits 0 and prune when a coin exceeds the remainder.
complexity: Exponential in worst case, O(T) stack

title: Bit strings with no 11
statement: List every binary string of length n that does not contain two adjacent 1s, in increasing order, one per line.
input: One integer n.
output: One string per line.
hints: You may only place a 1 if the previous character is not 1.
Try 0 first so the output is sorted.
approach: Backtrack position by position, always allowing 0 and allowing 1 only if the previous character is not 1.

title: All upper/lower variants
statement: Given a string of letters and digits, list every string obtained by choosing upper or lower case for each letter independently. Digits stay as they are. For each letter, the lower-case choice is explored before the upper-case one.
input: One string of letters and digits.
output: One variant per line, in the explored order.
hints: Only letters branch; digits are copied.
Process characters left to right.
approach: Recurse over positions, branching into lower and upper case for letters and copying other characters. Emit at the end of the string.

title: Count the self-avoiding walks
statement: A small grid has . for open cells and # for walls. Count the different routes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell that move up, down, left or right through open cells and never visit the same cell twice.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: One integer: the number of routes.

examples.why: Only the middle row links left and right: one route.

hints: Mark a cell visited when you enter it and unmark when you leave.
Reaching the destination counts one route; stop exploring from there.
approach: DFS with a visited set: from each cell try the four neighbors that are open and unvisited; count each arrival at the target; unmark on return.

title: Ways up the staircase
statement: A staircase has n steps and you climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count the distinct sequences of moves that land exactly on step n, modulo 1 000 000 007.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer: the number of ways modulo 1 000 000 007.
hints: To land on step n you came from n-1 or n-2.
That is the Fibonacci recurrence; keep only two values.
approach: ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2] with ways[0] = ways[1] = 1, iterated with a rolling pair and reduced modulo 1e9+7.

title: Cheapest way up the stairs
statement: Each step i of a staircase has a fee c[i] charged when you leave that step by climbing 1 or 2 steps. You may start standing on step 0 or step 1, and you finish when you are beyond the last step. Find the minimum total fee.
input: First line n; second line n non-negative fees.
output: One integer: the minimum total fee.

examples.why: Start on step 1 (fee 15) and jump past the end: 15.
Leave steps 0, 2 and 4 with two-step jumps: 1+1+1 = 3.

hints: Let best[i] be the cheapest cost to be standing at position i without paying i's fee yet.
best[i] = min(best[i-1] + c[i-1], best[i-2] + c[i-2]).
approach: dp over positions 0..n with dp[0] = dp[1] = 0; the answer is dp[n], the cost of reaching the top beyond the last step.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space with rolling values

title: Pick houses, skip neighbors
statement: Along a street, house i holds a[i] coins. You may collect from any set of houses as long as no two chosen houses are adjacent. Find the maximum coins you can collect.
input: First line n; second line n non-negative integers.
output: One integer: the maximum total.

examples.why: Take 2 and 9 for 11; 7 and 3 gives only 10.

hints: For house i either skip it or take it and skip i-1.
best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + a[i]).
approach: Rolling dp over houses keeping the best total including up to i-1 and i-2, updated with max(skip, take).

title: Fewest coins for the amount
statement: A shop accepts n coin values with unlimited supply of each. Find the minimum number of coins whose values add up to exactly T, or -1 if it is impossible. Do not assume that greedy works for these values.
input: First line n T; second line n positive coin values.
output: The minimum coin count, or -1.

examples.why: Odd amount cannot be made from 2s.

hints: Let best[x] be the fewest coins for amount x.
best[x] = 1 + min over coins c ≤ x of best[x-c].
approach: Bottom-up dp array of size T+1 with best[0] = 0 and infinity elsewhere; for each amount try every coin. Answer is best[T] or -1.

title: Paths around the rocks
statement: A hiker walks from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down. Cells marked # are rocks and cannot be entered; . cells are free. Count the distinct routes modulo 1 000 000 007.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: One integer: the number of routes modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: Two routes go around the rock in the center.

hints: Routes into a cell = routes into the cell above + routes into the cell to its left.
A rock cell always has 0 routes.
approach: dp[i][j] = 0 if rock else dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], seeded with dp[0][0] = 1 (if free). Reduce modulo 1e9+7.
complexity: O(R·C) time, O(C) space with a rolling row

title: Cheapest walk across the grid
statement: Every cell of an R by C grid has a toll. Starting at the top-left and moving only right or down, you must reach the bottom-right cell. You pay the toll of every cell you stand on, including the first and the last. Find the minimum total toll.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C non-negative integers.
output: One integer: the minimum total toll.
hints: You can only arrive from above or from the left.
Take the cheaper of the two predecessors.
approach: dp[i][j] = toll[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) with border cells using the single available predecessor.

title: Best streak of the week
statement: A shop records its daily profit (possibly negative) for n days. Find the largest total profit achievable over a non-empty run of consecutive days.
input: First line n; second line n integers.
output: One integer: the maximum sum of a contiguous non-empty subarray.

examples.why: All losses: the best is just -1.

hints: Decide at each day whether to extend the previous streak or start fresh.
cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]).
approach: Kadane's algorithm: keep the best sum of a streak ending at the current day and the global best over all days.

title: Tile a 2-by-n floor
statement: A hallway floor is 2 rows by n columns. You have unlimited 1-by-2 dominoes, which can lie flat or stand upright. Count the ways to tile the floor completely, modulo 1 000 000 007.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer: the number of tilings modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: Three upright; upright then a flat pair; flat pair then upright.

hints: Look at the leftmost column: it is covered by an upright domino or by two flat ones.
That leaves a floor of width n-1 or n-2.
approach: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) with f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2. Compute iteratively with two variables modulo 1e9+7.

title: Split into dictionary words
statement: Given a string without spaces and a dictionary of words, decide whether the string can be split into a sequence of dictionary words. Words may be used any number of times.
input: First line the string; second line k; then k dictionary words, one per line.
output: YES if a split exists, otherwise NO.
hints: ok[i] means the first i characters can be split.
ok[i] is true if some earlier ok[j] is true and w[j:i] is a word.
approach: Boolean dp over prefixes with ok[0] = true; for each end i test every split j with a set lookup. Answer is ok[n].
complexity: O(n²) substring checks (times word length), O(n) space

title: Split into equal halves
statement: Given n positive integers, decide whether they can be divided into two groups (every number in exactly one group) with the same sum.
input: First line n; second line n positive integers.
output: YES if such a split exists, otherwise NO.

examples.why: 11 on one side, 1+5+5 on the other.
Total 8 halves to 4, which is unreachable.

hints: If the total is odd the answer is immediately NO.
Now ask whether some subset sums to total/2.
approach: Subset-sum dp: boolean array up to total/2, updating from high to low for each number. Answer is dp[total/2].

title: Find the lonely badge
statement: Every visitor badge at a conference is scanned once on entry and once on exit, so each badge id appears exactly twice in the log, except one visitor who never left. Find the id of the badge that appears only once.
input: First line n (odd), second line n badge ids.
output: The single badge id that appears once.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5, n odd; ids are non-negative and fit in 32 bits

examples.why: 9 is the only id without a partner
a lone entry is the answer

hints: What is x XOR x? What is x XOR 0?
XOR is commutative and associative, so pairs cancel regardless of order.
approach: XOR all values together; paired values cancel to zero and the unpaired one remains.

title: Count the lit switches
statement: A control panel stores the state of 32 switches in a single non-negative integer, where bit i is 1 if switch i is on. Report how many switches are on. Try to do it without converting to a string.
input: A single integer n.
output: The number of 1 bits in n.
hints: Subtracting 1 from a number flips its lowest set bit and everything below it.
n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit; count how many times you can do that.
approach: Repeatedly apply n &= n-1 and count iterations until n is zero (Kernighan's trick).
complexity: O(k) time where k is the number of set bits, O(1) space

title: Crate stacking sizes
statement: A warehouse only accepts crates whose side length is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...). Given a side length, say whether it is acceptable. Use a bit trick rather than a loop of divisions.
input: A single integer n.
output: YES if n is a power of two, otherwise NO.
hints: A power of two has exactly one set bit.
Negative numbers and zero are never powers of two; check them first.
approach: Return n > 0 and (n & (n-1)) == 0, since clearing the only set bit leaves zero.

title: How many switches differ
statement: Two control panels each store their switch states as an integer. Count the switches whose state differs between the two panels, i.e. the number of bit positions where the two numbers disagree.
input: Two integers a and b on one line.
output: The number of differing bit positions.
hints: Which operation gives 1 exactly where two bits differ?
Count the ones in the result.
approach: Compute a XOR b and count its set bits.

title: Mirror the 32-bit word
statement: A legacy device sends 32-bit words with the bit order flipped: bit 0 should become bit 31, bit 1 should become bit 30, and so on. Given an unsigned 32-bit value, output the value with its bits mirrored.
input: One unsigned integer n.
output: The mirrored unsigned integer.
hints: Build the result one bit at a time: shift the result left, then add the lowest bit of n.
Do this exactly 32 times, even if n runs out of ones early.
approach: Loop 32 times: result = (result << 1) | (n & 1); n >>= 1. Mask to 32 bits if the language has wider integers.

title: Single-switch walk
statement: A panel with n switches must visit all 2^n switch configurations, changing exactly one switch between consecutive configurations, starting from all-off. Output the configurations as integers using the standard reflected Gray code order, where element i is i XOR (i >> 1).
input: A single integer n.
output: 2^n integers separated by spaces.
hints: Look at the formula in the statement; no search is needed.
Check: consecutive outputs differ in exactly one bit.
approach: Emit i ^ (i >> 1) for i from 0 to 2^n - 1.

title: Backpack subsets
statement: You have n items with given weights and a backpack that can carry at most K units. Count how many subsets of items (including the empty one) have a total weight not exceeding K. Enumerate subsets with a bitmask.
input: First line n and K, second line n weights.
output: The number of subsets with total weight at most K.
hints: Each integer from 0 to 2^n - 1 describes one subset: bit i says whether item i is taken.
Sum weights for the set bits and compare to K.
approach: Loop over all masks, sum the weights of set bits, and count those within the limit.
edgeCases: K = 0 leaves only the empty subset

title: Lowest lit switch
statement: Given a positive integer describing which switches are on, find the lowest switch that is on. Print its value as a power of two, and its index counting from 0 at the least significant bit.
input: A single positive integer n.
output: Two integers: the isolated lowest set bit value and its index.

examples.why: 40 = 101000, lowest set bit is 8 at index 3 -> '8 3'

hints: In two's complement, -n flips all bits above the lowest set bit.
n & -n keeps only that lowest bit.
approach: Compute low = n & -n; the index is the number of trailing zeros, i.e. log2(low).
edgeCases: n is a power of two

title: Swap neighbouring bits
statement: A 32-bit word must be fixed by swapping every even-position bit with its odd neighbour: bit 0 with bit 1, bit 2 with bit 3, and so on up to bits 30 and 31. Output the repaired value.
input: One unsigned integer n.
output: The word after swapping.
hints: Build two masks: one that selects even-position bits, one that selects odd-position bits.
Shift the even bits left, the odd bits right, and OR them.

title: Longest streak of ones
statement: A status register records an on/off flag per minute as the bits of an integer. Find the length of the longest run of consecutive 1 bits in its binary form.
input: One non-negative integer n.
output: The length of the longest run of 1s.
hints: Walk through bits while tracking the current run and the best run so far.
A trick: n &= n << 1 shortens every run by one; count how many steps until n is 0.
approach: Repeat n &= (n << 1) and count steps until n becomes 0; the count is the longest run.

title: Digital root of a giant
statement: Keep replacing a number with the sum of its decimal digits until a single digit remains; that digit is its digital root. The number may have up to 100000 digits, so it arrives as text. Find the result without simulating the repeated sums.
input: One line with a non-negative decimal number, no leading zeros except for 0 itself.
output: The digital root.
hints: Compare a number with its digit sum modulo 9.
Zero is special; multiples of 9 map to 9.
approach: A number is congruent to its digit sum mod 9, so the root is 0 for 0, else 1 + (n - 1) mod 9. Compute n mod 9 by summing digits of the string.
complexity: O(d) time for d digits, O(1) space

title: Zeros at the end of n!
statement: The factorial n! = 1·2·...·n gets very long. Count how many zeros appear at the end of its decimal representation, without computing the factorial.
input: One integer n.
output: The number of trailing zeros of n!.
hints: A trailing zero comes from a factor pair 2·5; factors of 2 are plentiful.
Count factors of 5, including those hidden in 25, 125, ...
approach: Sum floor(n/5) + floor(n/25) + floor(n/125) + ... until the term is zero.

title: Vault code power
statement: A vault code is a^b taken modulo m, where b can be astronomically large. Implement fast modular exponentiation (square-and-multiply) and print the code.
input: Three integers a, b, m on one line.
output: a^b mod m.
hints: Use the binary expansion of b: square the base each step and multiply into the result when the bit is 1.
Reduce modulo m after every multiplication; beware m = 1.
approach: Iterate over the bits of b, maintaining base = base^2 mod m and multiplying result by base when the bit is set. Start with result = 1 mod m.

title: Two square tiles
statement: A tiler has two square tiles with whole-number side lengths a and b (a, b ≥ 0). Can the total area a² + b² equal exactly n? Answer YES or NO.
input: One integer n.
output: YES or NO.

examples.why: no pair of squares sums to 21

hints: Loop a from 0 while a² ≤ n/2 and test whether n - a² is a perfect square.
Use integer square roots to avoid floating-point errors for large n.
approach: Iterate a up to sqrt(n/2) and check whether n - a² is a perfect square using an integer square root.

title: One row of Pascal
statement: Pascal's triangle begins with row 0 = [1], row 1 = [1, 1], row 2 = [1, 2, 1], where every inner entry is the sum of the two entries above it. Print row k without building all earlier rows from scratch if you can.
input: One integer k.
output: Row k, entries separated by spaces.
hints: Entry i of row k is C(k, i).
C(k, i+1) = C(k, i) * (k - i) / (i + 1), always an exact integer.
approach: Start with 1 and update each next entry by multiplying by (k - i) and dividing by (i + 1) with integer arithmetic.

title: Does the chain reach one
statement: Start with a positive integer and repeatedly replace it by the sum of the squares of its digits. If the process ever reaches 1 the number is called cheerful; otherwise it loops forever. Decide whether n is cheerful.
input: One integer n.
output: YES if the process reaches 1, otherwise NO.
hints: The numbers never grow large after the first step, so a loop must repeat a value.
Remember values you have seen, or use Floyd's cycle detection.
approach: Iterate the digit-square-sum map, storing seen values in a set; stop at 1 (YES) or on a repeat (NO).
complexity: O(log n) time per step, a small number of steps

title: Hailstone champion
statement: From a start value, repeat: if the number is even halve it, otherwise triple it and add one, until it reaches 1. The number of steps is the start's flight length. Among all starts from 1 to n-1, find the one with the longest flight (smallest start on ties) and report it with its length.
input: One integer n.
output: Two integers: the start value and its step count.
hints: Intermediate values can exceed 32 bits for larger n; use 64-bit integers.
Cache flight lengths of values you have already computed to avoid repeating work.
approach: Compute the length for each start with memoization on values below n, taking the maximum with a strict comparison so the smallest start wins ties.
complexity: O(n * average path) time, O(n) space

title: Divisible by either
statement: How many integers between 1 and n inclusive are divisible by a, by b, or by both? Remember not to count the numbers divisible by both twice.
input: Three integers n, a, b on one line.
output: The count.

examples.why: every multiple of 4 is already a multiple of 2 -> 5

hints: Count multiples of a, add multiples of b, subtract multiples of lcm(a, b).
lcm(a,b) = a / gcd(a,b) * b.
approach: Inclusion-exclusion: floor(n/a) + floor(n/b) - floor(n/lcm(a,b)).

title: Print in any base
statement: Convert a non-negative integer to a given base from 2 to 16 using digits 0-9 and uppercase A-F. Do it by hand with repeated division rather than a built-in formatter.
input: Two integers n and b on one line.
output: The representation of n in base b.
hints: The remainder of n divided by b is the last digit.
Collect digits in reverse and flip them at the end.
approach: While n > 0, take n mod b as the next digit and divide n by b; reverse the collected digits. Special-case 0.

title: Gears: common factor and meeting point
statement: A machine has n gears with given tooth counts meshed in a chain of rotations. Find the greatest common divisor of all tooth counts and the least common multiple, which tells after how many teeth-steps all gears return to their start together.
input: First line n, second line n positive integers.
output: The GCD and the LCM separated by a space.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 20; 1 ≤ value ≤ 1000; the LCM fits in 64 bits
hints: gcd(a, b, c) = gcd(gcd(a, b), c).
lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b; divide first to avoid overflow.
approach: Fold gcd and lcm across the list using the Euclidean algorithm.
complexity: O(n log max) time, O(1) space

title: Prime census
statement: A town numbers its houses 1 to n, and only houses with a prime number get a mailbox. Count the mailboxes using the sieve of Eratosthenes.
input: One integer n.
output: The count of primes not exceeding n.
hints: Cross out multiples of each prime starting from its square.
You only need to sieve with primes up to sqrt(n).
approach: Run the sieve of Eratosthenes with a boolean array and count the surviving indices ≥ 2.
complexity: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space

title: Prime recipe
statement: Write a number as a product of primes in increasing order, using ^ for repeated primes and ' * ' between factors, e.g. 360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5. For 1 print 1.
input: One integer n.
output: The factorization string.
hints: Trial-divide by candidates p while p*p ≤ n.
Whatever remains above 1 after the loop is a prime factor.
approach: Divide out each p from 2 upward while p² ≤ n counting exponents; append any leftover n > 1 as a prime.

title: How many divisors
statement: A teacher wants to split a class of n students into equal groups. Count how many group sizes (divisors of n, including 1 and n) are possible.
input: One integer n.
output: The number of positive divisors of n.
hints: Divisors come in pairs (d, n/d); you only need to scan up to sqrt(n).
Or use the exponent form: multiply (e+1) over the prime factorization.
approach: Factorize n and multiply (exponent + 1) for each prime, or scan d up to sqrt(n) counting pairs.

title: Smallest Goldbach split
statement: Every even number above 2 is believed to be the sum of two primes. For a given even n, find the pair p ≤ q of primes with p + q = n and the smallest p.
input: One even integer n.
output: p and q separated by a space.
hints: Test primality with a sieve up to n.
Scan p upward and stop at the first p with both p and n - p prime.
approach: Sieve primes up to n, then scan p from 2 until sieve[p] and sieve[n-p] are both true.
complexity: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space

title: Abundant numbers
statement: A number is abundant if the sum of its proper divisors (divisors smaller than itself) is larger than the number. 12 is abundant since 1+2+3+4+6 = 16. Count abundant numbers from 1 to n.
input: One integer n.
output: How many integers in [1, n] are abundant.
hints: Instead of factoring each number, add every d to all of its multiples.
A sieve-like loop over d and multiples runs in O(n log n).
approach: For each d from 1 to n/2, add d to the divisor sum of every multiple 2d, 3d, ...; then count indices whose sum exceeds the index.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
edgeCases: Perfect numbers like 6 are not abundant

title: Whole-number right triangles
statement: Count triples of positive integers (a, b, c) with a ≤ b, a² + b² = c² and c ≤ n. Each side must be a whole number, e.g. (3, 4, 5).
input: One integer n.
output: The number of such triples.
hints: Try all a ≤ b with b < n and test whether a² + b² is a perfect square no greater than n².
An integer square root avoids float errors.
approach: Brute force over pairs (a, b) with an integer square-root check is fast enough; alternatively generate primitive triples with Euclid's formula and scale them.

title: Pairs that add up evenly
statement: Count pairs of positions i < j in an array whose values add up to a multiple of k. Group values by their remainder mod k instead of checking every pair.
input: First line n and k, second line n integers.
output: The number of pairs.
hints: Two numbers with remainders r and (k - r) mod k combine to a multiple of k.
Remainders 0 (and k/2 when k is even) pair among themselves.
approach: Count values per remainder. For r < k - r multiply counts of r and k - r; for r = 0 and r = k/2 add c·(c-1)/2.

title: Twin lanterns
statement: Two primes that differ by exactly 2 (like 11 and 13) are twin primes. Count the twin pairs (p, p+2) where both numbers are at most n.
input: One integer n.
output: The number of twin prime pairs with p + 2 ≤ n.
hints: Sieve once up to n.
Then count p where both sieve[p] and sieve[p+2] are prime.
approach: Build a sieve up to n and count indices p with p and p + 2 both prime and p + 2 ≤ n.
complexity: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space

title: Robot on a doormat
statement: A vacuum robot starts at (0, 0) and follows a string of commands: U moves up (y+1), D down, L left (x-1), R right. Report where it ends and whether it ended on its starting spot.
input: One line of commands made of U, D, L, R.
output: Final x, final y, then YES if back at the origin otherwise NO, separated by spaces.

examples.why: net movement is zero in both axes -> '0 0 YES'

hints: Keep two integers and update them per command.
Only the final position matters, not the path.
approach: Walk through the commands updating x and y, then compare with zero.
edgeCases: Returns to origin midway but not at the end

title: Circle elimination
statement: n children stand in a circle numbered 1..n. Starting at child 1, count k children (including the starting one) and send the k-th home, then continue counting from the next child. The last child left wins. Which number wins?
input: Two integers n and k.
output: The number of the last remaining child.
hints: With n up to 10^5 and a list, deletions cost O(n) each; consider a recurrence instead.
If W(m) is the winner's 0-based index among m children, W(m) = (W(m-1) + k) mod m.
approach: Use the Josephus recurrence: r = 0; for m from 2 to n, r = (r + k) mod m; the answer is r + 1.

title: What colour is the light
statement: A traffic light cycles GREEN for g seconds, YELLOW for y seconds, then RED for r seconds, repeating forever, starting a green phase at second 0. What colour is showing during second t (the interval [t, t+1))?
input: Four integers g, y, r, t on one line.
output: GREEN, YELLOW or RED.
hints: The pattern repeats every g + y + r seconds.
Reduce t modulo the cycle and compare against thresholds.
approach: Compute c = t mod (g + y + r); GREEN if c < g, YELLOW if c < g + y, else RED.

title: Elevator odometer
statement: An elevator starts at floor s and serves requests strictly in the given order, moving one floor per unit of distance. Compute the total number of floors it travels.
input: First line m and s, second line m requested floors.
output: Total floors travelled.
hints: Keep the current floor and add absolute differences.
Repeated requests cost nothing.
approach: Iterate through requests adding |next - current| and updating current.

title: Pinball in a corridor
statement: A ball moves along a corridor of length L (positions 0..L) at v units per second, starting at position pos and heading towards L. When it hits an end it bounces back with the same speed. Where is it after t seconds? Positions are whole numbers.
input: Four integers L, pos, v, t on one line.
output: The ball's position after t seconds.

examples.why: goes to 10, comes back 3 units to 7

hints: Unfold the corridor: imagine the ball moves straight on a line of period 2L.
Fold the unfolded coordinate back: x if x ≤ L else 2L - x.
approach: Compute x = (pos + v·t) mod 2L; the answer is x if x ≤ L else 2L - x.

title: Vending machine change
statement: A vending machine has limited coins: pennies (1), nickels (5), dimes (10) and quarters (25). To return a given amount it uses as many quarters as it can, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies, never exceeding the stock of any coin. Print how many of each it returns, or IMPOSSIBLE if it cannot pay the exact amount.
input: First line the amount; second line four stock counts for pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters.
output: Four counts (pennies nickels dimes quarters) or IMPOSSIBLE.

examples.why: two quarters, one dime, one nickel, three pennies -> 3 1 1 2
only one dime is available -> IMPOSSIBLE

hints: Process coins from largest to smallest and take min(stock, remaining // value).
If the remainder is non-zero at the end the machine cannot make change.
approach: Greedy pass over denominations from high to low taking as many as stock allows; check that the remainder ends at zero.

title: Spiral staircase numbering
statement: Fill an n × n grid with the numbers 1 to n² in a clockwise spiral that starts at the top-left cell and goes right first, turning clockwise whenever the next cell is outside the grid or already filled. Print the grid.
input: One integer n.
output: n lines each with n space-separated integers.
hints: Keep a direction vector and rotate it clockwise with (dr, dc) -> (dc, -dr).
Turn when the next cell is out of bounds or already non-zero.
approach: Walk from (0,0) with direction right, writing 1..n², turning clockwise when blocked.
edgeCases: Odd n ends in the centre

title: Ants on a plank
statement: Ants walk at speed 1 on a plank of length L. Each ant's start position is given, and every ant walks either left or right but you do not know which. Ants that meet turn around instantly, and an ant leaves when it reaches either end. What is the longest time until the plank is guaranteed empty in the worst case of directions? (Meeting ants swapping directions is the same as passing through each other.)
input: First line n and L, second line n integer positions in [0, L].
output: The earliest time by which the plank is guaranteed empty.

examples.why: distances to the far end are 8, 5 and 9; the ant at 9 may need 9
the ant at 0 must walk the whole plank -> 7

hints: Pretend ants pass through each other; the set of positions is identical.
Each ant independently leaves after at most max(x, L - x).
approach: Treat collisions as pass-throughs; the answer is the maximum over ants of max(x, L - x).

title: Chop an expression into tokens
statement: Write a tokenizer for arithmetic text. Tokens are non-negative integers and the single characters + - * / ( ). Spaces may appear anywhere between tokens but never inside a number. Output the tokens in order, separated by one space.
input: One line containing digits, the operators + - * / ( ) and spaces.
output: The tokens separated by single spaces.
hints: Scan with an index: skip spaces; if the character is a digit, consume all following digits.
Every other non-space character is a token by itself.
approach: Single left-to-right scan: gather maximal digit runs into number tokens, emit operator characters individually, skip whitespace.

title: Calculator without brackets
statement: Evaluate an expression made of non-negative integers and the operators + - * /, with usual precedence (multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, left to right) and integer division that rounds towards zero. There are no brackets and no negative literals.
input: One line with the expression, spaces allowed.
output: The integer result.
constraints: Length ≤ 10^4; no division by zero; intermediate values fit in 64 bits
hints: Keep a running total and the current product/quotient term.
When you see + or -, finish the current term and add it to the total with its sign.
approach: Scan tokens: keep a 'term' that multiplies or divides as you go, and flush it into the total when a + or - arrives (using the sign of the previous such operator).
edgeCases: Long chains of the same operator

title: Pack runs of letters
statement: Compress a string by replacing every maximal run of equal characters with its length followed by the character, so aaabcc becomes 3a1b2c. Letters only; always write the count, even when it is 1.
input: One lowercase string.
output: The run-length encoded string.
hints: Walk with two indices: start of the run and a scanner that advances while characters match.
Emit the length (which can have several digits) then the character.
approach: Scan the string, extending each run, and append count + character to the output.

title: Unpack run-length text
statement: Decode a string made of pairs (count, letter) such as 3a1b2c back to aaabcc. The count can have several digits and is at least 1.
input: One encoded string.
output: The decoded string.
constraints: The decoded length is at most 10^6
hints: Read digits until you hit a letter; that number is the repeat count.
Append the letter that many times and continue after it.
approach: Parse the number greedily over consecutive digits, then repeat the next letter that many times.

title: Decode a form string
statement: Web forms send data as name=value pairs joined by &, where a space is written as + and any byte can be written as %XX with two hex digits (ASCII only here). Decode the string and print each pair on its own line as name=value. A pair with no = has an empty value.
input: One line with the encoded form string.
output: One decoded name=value pair per line, in order.
constraints: Length ≤ 10^5; escapes are valid and encode ASCII
hints: Split on & first, then on the first = in each pair, and only then decode each half.
Decoding: + becomes a space, %XX becomes the character with that hex code.
approach: Split into pairs on &, split each at the first =, and decode each part with a scan converting + to space and %XX to the corresponding character.

title: Duration to seconds
statement: A duration is written as a sequence of number+unit parts such as 1d2h30m5s, where units are d (86400 seconds), h (3600), m (60) and s (1). Units may appear in any order and each at most once. Convert it to total seconds.
input: One duration string.
output: Total seconds.
hints: Read a run of digits, then one letter; multiply and add.
Use a lookup table for unit multipliers.
