approach: Scan the string: accumulate digits into a number, and when a unit letter appears add number × multiplier to the total and reset the number.

title: camelCase to snake_case
statement: Convert an identifier from camelCase to snake_case: every uppercase letter becomes its lowercase form preceded by an underscore. The input has only letters and starts with a lowercase letter.
input: One identifier.
output: The snake_case identifier.
hints: Check each character; if it is uppercase, insert an underscore first.
Lowercase the letter before appending.
approach: Iterate the characters, emitting '_' plus the lowercase letter for uppercase ones and the letter itself otherwise.

title: Read a Roman numeral
statement: Convert a valid Roman numeral to an integer. Symbols: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted (IV = 4, XC = 90).
input: One Roman numeral.
output: The integer value.
hints: Compare each symbol with the one that follows it.
If it is smaller than the next, subtract it; otherwise add it.
approach: Scan left to right adding each symbol's value, but subtract it when the next symbol is larger.

title: Which version is newer
statement: Compare two dotted version strings such as 1.10.2 and 1.9. Compare numerically part by part from the left; a missing part counts as 0, so 1.0 equals 1.0.0. Print 1 if the first is newer, -1 if the second is newer, 0 if equal.
input: Two version strings separated by a space.
constraints: Each version has 1 to 10 parts; each part ≤ 10^6
hints: Split on dots and convert each part to an integer; comparing as text would put 10 before 9.
Pad the shorter list with zeros.
approach: Split both versions, convert to integers, pad the shorter with zeros, and compare lexicographically.

title: Tally the log levels
statement: Each log line looks like HH:MM:SS [LEVEL] message words..., for example 12:03:44 [WARN] disk almost full. Count how many lines carry each level and print the levels in alphabetical order with their counts. Ignore the message text, even if it contains brackets.
input: Several log lines, one per line.
output: One line per level present: the level, a space, and its count, sorted alphabetically.
hints: The level is the first bracketed word after the timestamp.
Count with a dictionary and sort the keys at the end.
approach: Extract the bracketed level token from each line (the second space-separated token), increment a counter, then output sorted by key.
complexity: O(n + k log k) time, O(k) space

title: Fill the template
statement: A template contains placeholders written as {name}. Replace each placeholder with the value from a list of name=value definitions. Placeholders whose name is not defined stay exactly as written. Substituted values are not scanned again for placeholders.
input: First line the template; following lines are name=value definitions.
output: The completed text.
constraints: Template length ≤ 10^4; ≤ 100 definitions; names are letters, digits or underscore
hints: Scan for '{' then read up to the next '}' to get the name.
Look the name up; if missing, copy the placeholder back unchanged.
approach: One pass over the template: copy ordinary characters, and when a well-formed {name} appears, output the mapped value or the original text if the name is undefined.
complexity: O(n + total value length) time, O(n) space

title: C: reverse with two pointers
statement: In C, write void reverse(int *lo, int *hi) that reverses the elements from *lo to *hi inclusive, in place, using only pointer arithmetic and a swap through pointers (no array indexing inside the function). Read an array of n ints into a malloc'ed buffer, call your function, print the result and free the buffer.
input: First line n, second line n integers.
output: The reversed array separated by spaces.

examples.why: a single element is its own reverse

hints: Move lo forward and hi backward until they meet.
Swap with a temporary: int t = *lo; *lo = *hi; *hi = t;
approach: Loop while lo < hi: swap *lo and *hi, then lo++ and hi--. The comparison of two pointers into the same array is well defined.

title: C: a buffer that grows
statement: In C, read integers from standard input until end of file; you do not know how many there are. Store them in a heap array that starts with capacity 4 and doubles with realloc when full. Print the sum, the maximum and the count, then free the array. Always check realloc's result.
input: Whitespace-separated integers until EOF (at least one).
output: Sum, maximum and count separated by spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ count ≤ 10^6; values fit in 32 bits, sum fits in 64 bits
hints: Keep three variables: pointer, size, capacity. When size == capacity, double capacity and realloc.
Assign realloc's result to a temporary first so you do not lose the old pointer on failure.
approach: Loop with scanf; grow the buffer geometrically (capacity *= 2) when full; accumulate sum and max; free the buffer at the end.

title: C++: RAII guard order
statement: In C++, write a class Guard whose constructor prints 'acquire NAME' and whose destructor prints 'release NAME'. Read n names, create one Guard per name inside a single block scope (store them in a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Guard>> built in order), and let the scope end. Releases must happen in the reverse order of acquisition; do not rely on the vector's own destruction order, instead pop the vector from the back one element at a time.
input: First line n, then n names, one per line.
output: n 'acquire' lines in input order, then n 'release' lines in reverse order.

examples.out:
acquire db
acquire file
release file
release db
examples.why: acquire db / acquire file / release file / release db

hints: Stack-allocated locals are destroyed in reverse order of declaration; a vector's order is not something to rely on.
Call pop_back in a loop: each pop destroys the unique_ptr and so runs the destructor.
approach: Create guards in order, then pop_back until the vector is empty so destructors run last-in first-out; this mirrors what automatic scope exit does for separate local variables.
edgeCases: Exceptions should still release (destructors run during unwinding)

title: C++: sort with a lambda
statement: In C++, read n words and sort them with std::sort and a lambda comparator: shorter words first, and words of equal length in alphabetical order. Print one word per line. Do not write a separate comparator function.
input: First line n, then n words one per line.
output: The sorted words, one per line.
hints: The lambda takes two const std::string& and returns true if the first should come before the second.
Compare sizes first and fall back to operator< on equal sizes.
approach: std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const std::string& a, const std::string& b){ return a.size() != b.size() ? a.size() < b.size() : a < b; });

title: Rust: lifetimes in a helper
statement: In Rust, write fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str that returns the longer of two string slices (the first if they have equal length). Read n lines each holding two words, call the function on borrowed slices of the input (without cloning) and print the result for each line.
input: First line n, then n lines of two words.
output: For each pair, the longer word (first on ties).

examples.why: moon, then ab (tie keeps the first)

hints: The returned reference must be tied to both inputs, hence the shared lifetime 'a.
Use split_whitespace on the line and pass the two slices directly.
approach: Declare both parameters and the return type with the same lifetime 'a, compare .len() and return a when a.len() >= b.len().
complexity: O(1) per call, O(n) input storage
edgeCases: Words borrowed from a String that lives long enough

title: Rust: dedup through &mut
statement: In Rust, write fn dedup(words: &mut Vec<String>) that removes later duplicates in place, keeping the first occurrence of each word and the original order. Use a HashSet<String> of the words seen and Vec::retain, and call the function from main with a mutable borrow. Print the remaining words on one line.
input: First line n, then n words one per line.
output: The unique words in first-seen order separated by spaces.
hints: retain takes a closure that runs once per element in order and keeps those returning true.
HashSet::insert returns false when the value was already present.
approach: Create a HashSet, then words.retain(|w| seen.insert(w.clone())); the closure mutates the set while retain mutates the vector.

title: Rust: iterator chain
statement: In Rust, compute the sum of the squares of the even numbers in a list using only iterator adaptors (iter, filter, map, sum) and no for loop or mutable accumulator. Use i64 for the result.
input: First line n, second line n integers.
output: The sum of squares of even values.
hints: filter takes a closure over &&i64 when chained on iter(); you may need to dereference.
sum needs a type annotation such as ::<i64>.
approach: nums.iter().filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0).map(|&x| x * x).sum::<i64>().

title: Rust: HashMap entry API
statement: In Rust, count how often each word occurs in the input using HashMap and the entry API (*map.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1). Then collect the pairs into a Vec and sort them by count descending, ties alphabetically, and print 'word count' lines.
input: Whitespace-separated lowercase words, possibly over several lines.
output: One 'word count' line per distinct word in the required order.

examples.in: to be or not to be

hints: entry(key).or_insert(0) returns a mutable reference to the counter.
sort_by with then_with (or a tuple key with Reverse) handles the two-level ordering.
approach: Count with the entry API, move the map into a Vec<(String, usize)>, sort by (Reverse(count), word) and print.
complexity: O(n + k log k) time, O(k) space

title: Rust: your own Iterator
statement: In Rust, define struct Fib { a: u64, b: u64 } and implement the Iterator trait for it so that next() yields the Fibonacci numbers 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, ... forever. In main use take_while to print all values strictly below n on one line.
input: One integer n.
output: The Fibonacci numbers smaller than n separated by spaces (empty line if none).
hints: next returns Option<u64>; an infinite iterator always returns Some.
Use std::mem::replace or a tuple swap to advance the pair, mind overflow with checked_add or a limit on n.
approach: Implement Iterator with type Item = u64; next stores the current a, then advances (a, b) = (b, a + b), and returns Some(current). main chains Fib{a:0,b:1}.take_while(|&x| x < n).
edgeCases: Large n near the u64 limit

title: Go: three-stage pipeline
statement: In Go, build a pipeline of goroutines connected by channels: stage one generates the integers 1..n, stage two squares each number, stage three keeps only odd squares. The main goroutine prints what arrives, in order, one per line. Each stage must close its output channel when its input is exhausted.
input: One integer n.
output: The odd squares among 1², 2², ..., n², one per line.
hints: A function that returns <-chan int and starts a goroutine inside is a neat way to build a stage.
Use defer close(out) at the top of each stage's goroutine.
approach: Write gen(n), square(in) and oddOnly(in) functions that each create an output channel, start a goroutine that ranges over the input (or loop for gen), sends results and closes the output; main ranges over the last channel.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) buffered between stages
edgeCases: n = 2 where only 1 passes the filter

title: Python: lazy prime generator
statement: In Python, write a generator function primes() that yields the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, ... without end, remembering the primes found so far to test candidates. In main, use itertools.islice to print the first n primes on one line, without ever building a full list of the infinite sequence.
input: One integer n.
output: The first n primes separated by spaces.
hints: A function containing yield returns a generator object; calling next() resumes it where it paused.
Test a candidate only against stored primes up to its square root.
approach: Keep a list of found primes; loop over candidates starting at 2, yield a candidate if no stored prime p with p*p <= candidate divides it, and append it. islice(primes(), n) takes the prefix.
complexity: About O(n sqrt(p_n) / log) time, O(n) space
edgeCases: Generator must not be exhausted by earlier use

title: Python: dataclass inventory
statement: In Python, define a @dataclass Item with fields name (str), qty (int) and price (float) and a property or method value that returns qty * price. Read the items, sort them by value descending (ties by name) and print each item's name and value with two decimals, then a final TOTAL line with the combined value.
input: First line n, then n lines 'name qty price'.
output: One 'name value' line per item in sorted order, then 'TOTAL value'.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000; qty ≤ 1000; price ≤ 1000 with at most two decimals
hints: @dataclass generates __init__ and __repr__ for you from the annotated fields.
sorted(items, key=lambda i: (-i.value, i.name)) handles the two-level ordering.
approach: Parse each line into an Item, sort with a key of (-value, name), format with f'{v:.2f}' and accumulate the total.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Python: chunking generator
statement: In Python, write a generator chunks(iterable, k) that lazily yields successive lists of up to k items from any iterable (the last list may be shorter). Use it, with a generator expression or loop, to print the sum of each chunk of the input numbers on one line. Do not slice a pre-built list; consume the iterator.
input: First line n and k, second line n integers.
output: The chunk sums separated by spaces.
hints: Use itertools.islice(it, k) on a shared iterator, or append to a buffer and yield when it reaches size k.
After the loop, yield the leftover buffer if it is not empty.
approach: Create an iterator once; repeatedly take list(islice(it, k)) and yield it until it comes back empty.

title: Python: context managers nest
statement: In Python, write a context manager (a class with __enter__ and __exit__, or @contextlib.contextmanager) that prints 'enter NAME' when the with block starts and 'exit NAME' when it ends. Given a list of names, enter them all as nested with-blocks (use contextlib.ExitStack) and print their enter and exit lines. Exits must run in the reverse of the entering order.
input: First line n, then n lines 'open NAME'.
output: n 'enter' lines in order, then n 'exit' lines in reverse order.

examples.out:
enter a
enter b
exit b
exit a
examples.why: enter a / enter b / exit b / exit a

hints: ExitStack.enter_context registers a context and returns its value; leaving the stack's with-block unwinds them last-in first-out.
The exit lines should appear even if an exception happens inside the block.
approach: with ExitStack() as stack: for each name call stack.enter_context(Ctx(name)); when the stack's block ends, __exit__ is called on each entry in reverse order.
edgeCases: Exception inside the block still exits
